It has been revealed that not long ago, I drifted through a handful of old European cities. What stayed with me was neither the cathedrals nor the cafés with their thimbles of ferocious coffee.

It was the company the bronze kept: The squares belonged to poets and playwrights, astronomers and philosophers, figures in stone cloaks gazing over bustling pigeons as if weighing one more line. Here and there, a statesman sulked on his plinth, and the courthouses guarded their jurists, but officeholders were scarce.

The exception was the kings, those equestrian gentlemen forever reining in horses that never move.

Sources indicate that the pattern has a plausible explanation. Europe was hardly a stranger to electoral politics. Athenian citizens voted in assembly, the Roman Republic chose its consuls, Iceland’s Althing has convened since 930, and Venice elected its doges for roughly 11 centuries.

So, the scarcity of political monuments cannot be explained by the absence of voting. A better account is that a reputation lasts about as long as the work behind it remains usable.

>>> The Hidden Jewel at Jacksonville State.

Recent findings suggest that A literary or scientific achievement keeps functioning. Dante’s “Commedia,” Shakespeare’s plays, and Newton’s “Principia” can still be met directly, without an intermediary, and they answer questions each generation asks anew.

Recent findings suggest that A statesman’s achievement, by contrast, is tied to the circumstance that called it forth: a treaty, a succession crisis, a levy. Once that circumstance passes, the achievement survives chiefly as historical record. The principal lessons learned from political figures are the consequences of their decisions rather than the reasoning that produced them, which is seldom preserved and less often consulted.

Political monuments are also unusually exposed to revision. The removal of Lenin statues across the former Eastern Bloc after 1989, and the toppling of Edward Colston in Bristol in 2020, suggest that a statesman’s standing stays open to dispute in a way a poet’s rarely does. Southerners know this quite well, having watched Confederate monuments come down in town after town.

Sources indicate that which brings me home to Auburn, where the statuary has another temperament altogether. Ours wear shoulder pads. Heisman winners stride eternally outside Jordan-Hare, and Shug Jordan keeps his vigil.

I love a Saturday on the Plains as dearly as anyone alive. But an athlete’s fame is the briefest bloom in the garden, briefer even than a senator’s. Who toasts the champions of antiquity? The wrestlers and charioteers of Olympia survive mostly because Pindar wrote odes to them. They endure, in other words, by the grace of a poet.

So it was with a small, private gladness that I read the news: Auburn announced a $22 million investment from the state of Alabama, “championed by Gov. Kay Ivey, an Auburn alumna, to establish the Kay Ivey Institute for Civic Leadership.” At last, we may raise a monument to the kind of figure the Old World remembers.

Sources indicate that auburn enters a crowded and quickening field. Recently, I mentioned the civics centers popping up across many institutions and states. Ohio has committed $24 million to create civic-education centers at five public universities. The ones to beat are well known: Florida, with its Hamilton School for Classical and Civic Education; Texas, with its School of Civic Leadership and Civitas Institute; and Tennessee, whose Institute of American Civics was established in 2022 by the state’s general assembly.

These programs now count in the standings too, since City Journal’s new college-ranking system rewards institutions that host a School of Civic Thought. It’s high time, isn’t it, that Auburn’s name sat atop that list?

Of our own institute, we know very little. The university says its academic direction, programming and long-term priorities will be developed in the coming months, so my hopes go out wearing a raincoat.

>>> A Columbus Day Question—Have We Finally Stopped Distorting Our Past?

Still, the opportunity is plain. Auburn could gather some of the most distinguished and exacting scholars in the humanities: historians, political theorists, legal minds, and philosophers. Those disciplines are the timbers from which civic life is built.

In a recent development, the town’s growing. It’s a fine place to live and think, and its research already commands respect well beyond the state line.

The old oaks at Toomer’s Corner stood since the late 1930s. They died because of football. After Auburn beat Alabama in 2010, an aggrieved rival poured herbicide into their roots.

Recent findings suggest that their replacements fared little better. One was set ablaze during a celebration after a win over Louisiana State University, and the corner has been replanted more than once since.

Passion for a game can kill the very things it gathers around. Yet something survived. Saplings grown from the original oaks’ acorns now line the walk from the corner to Samford Hall. The descendants of those trees mark a path from the place where we celebrate to the place where we study.

Industry observers note that if the Ivey Institute is built with care, more of us may follow that path. Someday, a visitor may find, among the halfbacks, a philosopher in bronze. Better still, he may find generations of graduates who read the founders as eagerly as they read a box score.

That would be a monument no poison or match could take down.

Scott Proctor. “Alexander Scott Mercurio planned to attack that fundamental freedom by bringing death and destruction to several churches. This sentence reveals that the Department of Justice will relentlessly investigate, pursue, and prosecute those who would terrorize and murder Americans for exercising their religious rights.”.

Shirts for the District of Idaho. “Protecting our communities from terrorist activity is always the number one priority of this office and the Department of Justice. Industry observers note that this short latest article of mine has now been published in the Notre Dame Law Review. The Introduction:.

In a recent development, there are many crucial significant-picture questions about original meaning and the Free Speech, Free Press, Assembly, and Petition Clauses. This short Essay will leave those questions for others. Instead, it will offer as illustrations some specific, concrete questions—and, in some instances, answers—about original meaning and the freedom of expression. I hope these narrow illustrations can help us think about the broader questions.

From the table of contents, which should illustrate the subjects I cover:.

Industry observers note that I. Broad Evidence, and Silently Consistent Precedents A. "The Liberty of the Press Is Not Confined to Newspapers and Periodicals" B. Symbolic Expression C. Civil Liability II. Scant Evidence: Provoking a Riot III. Ambiguous Evidence: Enjoining Repetition of Libels.

Whether courts should shift the constitutional law of free expression to a more originalist footing is an crucial and difficult question. Perhaps it's a question that should be resolved entirely as a matter of constitutional theory—maybe such an approach is required by proper interpretive principles, or maybe it's forbidden by other principles (for instance, having to do with precedent).

Recent findings suggest that but it's also possible that the answer may rest in part on how practically usable an originalist framework is likely to be. And to consider that, it's helpful to have in mind some practical questions. Some are already familiar, for instance questions related to damages liability in libel cases, obscenity law, and the like. This short Essay has aimed to help supplement those familiar examples with some others that haven't been much discussed; I hope others who think about the topic can find them useful.

I expect I'll post excerpts from the article in the coming days.

Wall Street delivered its verdict on the blue-wave midterms 48 hours later in the form of a red wave—red ink, that is.

Sources indicate that after a brief relief rally the day after the election, the Dow shed more than 1,800 points, the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell more than 5% and into correction territory, and roughly $2.5 trillion in market value vanished in a single session. Nvidia alone dropped more than 8%.

Market participants watched the collapse of the AI trade in real time—the bet that a massive buildout of data centers, chips, and software would power faster growth, higher productivity and rising wages for years to come. That theory hit the brick wall of an incoming Congress that has AI and data centers on their blacklist.

According to recent reports, democrats, who will comfortably control the Senate and hold their largest House majority in nearly two decades, have been far more hostile to data centers and AI than Republicans have. Several of their biggest wins came in places such as Texas, where local opposition to newly introduced data centers had been building.

Investors can read the writing on the wall: more regulation and taxation, slower permitting, and lower profits for AI and AI-adjacent companies. Since equity prices are ultimately justified by future earnings, adjusting those future expectations down also drove down equity prices.

>>> What’s Really Behind the Call to Regulate AI.

The fallout goes well beyond Silicon Valley. AI investment has been a key component of recent growth, and tens of millions of ordinary Americans own these companies through their 401(k)s. A slower buildout means fewer construction jobs, less demand for electricians and engineers, and slower productivity gains that drive real wage growth.

The fiscal picture is dimmer, too. With Democrats running both chambers, there is no chance of further tax reform or meaningful spending cuts for at least two years. If a Republican Congress couldn't bring itself to enshrine the DOGE savings into law, a Democratic one certainly won't.

Instead, Democrat leaders are already promising to restore cost-increasing Obamacare subsidies and unwind recently implemented work-requirement reforms for welfare, all of which will layer upcoming commitments on top of deficits already running at levels once seen only in wartime or recession.

Aside from burdening future generations with debt, these perpetual deficits have consequences for Americans today. The government is crowding out borrowing in the private sector, competing with families and businesses for loanable funds, thereby driving up interest rates on everything from mortgages to student loans to credit cards.

It has been revealed that those higher borrower costs fall especially hard on those Americans that are already in debt and behind financially. The flood of government debt issuance also puts pressure on the Federal Reserve to help finance the debt by creating money to pay for perpetual deficits—a recipe for more inflation.

>>> Slowing Data Center Construction Signals the Need for Pro-Growth Reforms.

Unfortunately, a Democratic Congress will also likely offer no help on permitting reform, which is badly needed to build the pipelines, transmission lines and reliable power plants a growing economy requires.

So the outlook is clearly worse, but why isn’t it terrible? Much of the consequential economic public policy changes of the past two years didn't depend on Congress, and it won’t go forward either. And while the tax-reform legislation passed last year obviously did require Congress, most of its provisions are permanent and won’t need reauthorization.

Sources indicate that the administration retains broad authority to problem executive orders and roll back burdensome regulations. Cutting that red tape, on everything from energy production to banking, reduces compliance costs for Americans without a single vote on Capitol Hill.

Democrats will certainly try to slow that good work. Their leaders are already planning a wave of made-for-cable show trials that will drain time and attention from officials who should be dismantling the bureaucracy. But investigations can only delay regulatory reform, not stop it.

The president’s veto is another silver lining that will likely prevent the Democratic Congress from enacting sweeping tax hikes or newly introduced regulatory regimes. The worst ideas will hopefully die in committee or an Oval Office waste basket.

The economy has weathered worse than a hostile Congress. Ongoing deregulation and existing tax reform are still tailwinds for economic growth while the veto pen is there to stop headwinds as they arise. The outlook might be blue, but it’s not black and blue.

Mitigating shipbuilding risks, such as constrained production capacity and the integration of numerous advanced technologies, necessitate a continuous testing regimen that scales up as the ships are built.The U.S. Navy Could Use a Modern “Battlecruiser” WarshipThe unveiling of the battleship comes as the Navy faces the imminent loss of significant at-sea firepower. By 2031, the departures of various submarines, cruisers, and destroyers will see nearly 2,000 missile-launch tubes lost. Industry observers note that last December, President Donald Trump introduced his vision for the United States Navy: a 30-year shipbuilding initiative called the “Golden Fleet.” Flanking him during his unveiling of this plan were renderings of a core component of that future Navy: USS Defiant, the lead ship of a new, modern class of battleship. But delivering it faces significant hurdles. The first is realistically addressing the Navy’s shaky shipbuilding track record. The second is surviving the changed political reality in Washington—made more challenging by Trump’s original plan to name the class of warship after himself.

It has been revealed that by any name, the battleship addresses critical needs for the U.S. Navy. A modern battleship’s firepower, command and control, and data-fusion capabilities have been proven vital in recent conflicts in the Black Sea, the Red Sea, and the Persian Gulf. Mitigating shipbuilding risks, such as constrained production capacity and the integration of numerous advanced technologies, necessitate a continuous testing regimen that scales up as the ships are built.

The U.S. Navy Could Use a Modern “Battlecruiser” Warship.

In a recent development, the unveiling of the battleship comes as the Navy faces the imminent loss of significant at-sea firepower. By 2031, the departures of various submarines, cruisers, and destroyers will see nearly 2,000 missile-launch tubes lost. To blunt this loss, the next iteration of Virginia-class nuclear submarines will carry 28 hypersonic missiles, and the Navy’s unmanned vessels may also begin to carry offensive weapons.

Recent findings suggest that >>> The U.S. Navy Must Build the “Golden Fleet”.

Recent findings suggest that the Navy missed an opportunity to address this firepower dilemma with its aborted CG(X) next-generation cruiser program, abandoned in 2011. These forced aging destroyers and Ticonderoga-class cruisers to continue shouldering the air and missile defense responsibilities for carrier strike groups. Flight III Arleigh Burke-class destroyers, however, lack the firepower and crew to fully assume the cruiser mission. The Arleigh Burke-class has 96 missile tubes, against 122 on the Ticonderoga-class, and has limited berthing for the needed staff to manage air and missile defenses for the carrier strike group.

In the long term, the Defiant and subsequent battleships are intended to fill this mission and firepower gap. The Defiant, with its added firepower, sensors and crew, will take over the Ticonderoga-class warships’ responsibilities for defending carrier strike groups. The ship will also employ long-range hypersonic missiles in support of carrier air-strike operations to rapidly suppress emerging threats.

The combination of capabilities merged in Defiant with sustained high speeds makes the vessel more closely resemble a battlecruiser—a high-speed battleship able to deliver long-range firepower and defend the carrier strike group from air and missile threats. However, recent battle lessons are creating another critical mission.

The damage inflicted upon U.S. Fifth Fleet Headquarters in Bahrain, and its temporary evacuation due to Iranian missile releases, demonstrates the vulnerability of permanent land-based naval installations to air attack. Moving headquarters to sea is one way to mitigate this danger, and follows a long tradition of numbered fleet command ships. A battlecruiser with robust command and control capabilities can maintain a common operational picture with the warships and unmanned platforms of its numbered fleet, reducing the Navy’s reliance on global communications.

>>> To Build the Golden Fleet.

How the Defiant Can Clear the Political Minefield on Capitol Hill.

Sources indicate that while battlecruisers are needed now, the United States faces numerous constraints that must be navigated before they can join the Golden Fleet. The high build cost of these ships will likely stir substantial resistance from budget-conscious members of Congress; a bill estimated by the Congressional Budget Office to be upwards of $23 billion for the first and subsequent ships costing $18 billion each. There are also serious shortages of skilled workers capable of efficiently building such intricate and substantial ships. Moreover, establishing new or expanding existing shipyards to build these battlecruisers requires working through onerous shipbuilding regulations.

Keeping Congress’ support will necessitate reducing the potential for cost overruns and program delays. One way to accomplish this is to use proven technologies and systems in the initial design. Doing this would result in Defiant embracing existing systems to meet its mission requirements the soonest. Integrating systems like the hypersonic missile technologies being developed for the Zumwalt-class destroyers and the newly introduced AN/SPY-6 radars being installed in Arleigh Burke-class vessels will further compress production timelines.

In time, the design will need to be improved on through continuous updates—one being the transition to nuclear power to sustain high speeds and pace the aircraft carrier the battlecruiser is intended to protect. One option is using the same A1B nuclear power plant now used in the Ford-class aircraft carriers, given enough time for production to ramp up to support aircraft carrier and battlecruiser production.

According to recent reports, resurrecting the battlecruiser for modern naval missions is a highly ambitious initiative, and it may yet fall through. But it is needed to equip the U.S. Navy with the capabilities for fighting a modern naval war across the Pacific.

This piece originally appeared in The National Interest.

#44061. Block, Blunt, Break: NATO’s Newly introduced Theory of Victory

Block, Blunt, Break: NATO’s Newly introduced Theory of Victory

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On October 12, 2026, U.S. Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich, Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR), gave a speech at the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland in which he outlined NATO’s new theory of victory to deter and, if necessary, defeat Russian aggression.[REF] This theory of victory, called “Block, Blunt, Break,” centers on employing combined arms and maneuver to block initial enemy assaults on Alliance territory, blunt follow-on offensives, and, if necessary, break the enemy’s ability to sustain combat operations. SACEUR’s speech comes at a time of considerable consternation in Eastern European capitals after months of suspected Russian hybrid activities including drone incursions and sabotage. General Grynkewich’s deterrence-focused theory of victory struck the right tone, reassuring worried allies and signaling to Moscow that the United States and its NATO allies are confident of their ability to defeat a Russian incursion into a NATO state and that Russia would do well not to consider one. The speech and the strategy itself also appear wisely designed to avoid unnecessary escalation with Russia as SACEUR made clear throughout that NATO is a defensive Alliance.Block, Blunt, BreakGeneral Grynkewich said that a classified version of this new NATO strategy had been agreed on by all 32 members of the Alliance about three months before his October 12 speech.[REF] He explained his decision to present Block, Blunt, Break in public as a helpful measure to assuage increasingly anxious NATO populations vulnerable to evolving security threats.[REF] General Grynkewich summarized his theory of victory as follows: “We will block the initial attack. If the attack persists, we will blunt it and prevent enemy advance. And if required, we will break the enemy’s forces and the operational warfighting system that is arrayed against us.”[REF]Block. NATO land forces will meet any enemy assault with preponderant force at the point of contact and not trade territory for time. As these forces prevent adversaries from seizing Alliance territory, air and sea forces will gain superiority before aggressively supporting NATO forces on the ground. Space and cyber forces will be employed, creating a lattice of forces meant to prevent the enemy from holding its ground.Blunt. Following the block phase, NATO forces will focus on denying the enemy’s ability to generate offensive momentum. This effort will include expanded deployments of manned and autonomous forces across domains to maintain operational advantage. The mass employment of effects in the forward battlespace will overwhelm enemy formations, thereby disrupting any continued advance.Break. If the enemy continues its attack or employs reserves, NATO forces will expand operations to break the enemy’s broader warfighting system. NATO will apply mass pressure through all domains to break down the enemy’s ability to sustain its forces. A major contributing factor to this pressure campaign will be the pairing of precision munitions with sweeping volumes of attritable and affordable effects. These efforts will isolate enemy formations from replenishment and paralyze the command and control of the opposing force.[REF]Strategic ContextThis theory of victory is a marked shift from earlier NATO theories of victory, which focused on trading space for time—that is, allowing Russian forces to move into NATO territory, while NATO forces harass and slow Russian advances until decisive force can be brought to bear to destroy and then expel all Russian forces from NATO territory.Block, Blunt, Break is a significant change from NATO Cold War strategy.During the Cold War, West Germany was the NATO state considered most likely to be attacked by massive numbers of Soviet-led Warsaw Pact forces, and the Fulda Gap was often identified as the most likely attack route. The geographic size of West Germany meant that NATO forces could fall back tens or hundreds of kilometers before they could generate enough combat mass to begin a counteroffensive against Soviet and Warsaw Pact forces and then expel them from NATO soil. In this sense, NATO planned to trade territory for time, during which it would seize the conventional advantage.Today, the Suwalki Gap between Lithuania and Poland is often cited as the modern equivalent of the Fulda Gap, especially because it separates Russian-allied Belarus from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.[REF] The three Baltic States of Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania are for numerous reasons the NATO states against which full-scale Russian aggression is most likely; for example, Russian revanchists claim the existence of Russian-speaking minorities in Estonia and Latvia as a potential pretext, and Russian military planners could seek to connect the Russian exclave by land to either Belarus or Russia, and Lithuania is in their way. In the Baltic States, Block, Blunt, Break makes sense as the strategy for deterring or defending against Russian aggression from both a military planning and a political perspective.From a military planning perspective, the lack of strategic depth in Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania was likely a major factor in the change in strategy. Blocking the Russian advance from the outset prevents the Russians from gaining a foothold that may prove difficult to dislodge once fortified and reinforced.From a political perspective, Block, Blunt, Break reinforces allied cohesion in the face of Russian aggression against a Baltic state or some other frontline state. Should Russia rapidly gain lodgment within Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia, it could then sue for peace before NATO could dislodge Russian forces and liberate those three NATO members. This could well create real political divisions within the North Atlantic Council, in which some countries would press for the liberation of the Baltic States, while others may seek to accept the peace proposal. It is not inconceivable that such a development could lead to the fracturing and potential breakup of NATO—long a goal of Moscow. This new strategy articulated by SACEUR could be a way to defend every inch of NATO soil from the outset and prevent this difficult scenario.Strategic SignalsGeneral Grynkewich used his speech at the Warsaw Security Forum to demonstrate how NATO allies intend to prevent conflict and defeat aggression if needed. He stressed that NATO’s Block, Blunt, Break strategy is defensive and seeks to prevent enemies from achieving their offensive objectives. While detailing this theory of victory, General Grynkewich provided a vision for a future NATO with enhanced military strength, operational readiness, and a unified commitment to the defense of all the Alliance’s territory.This speech landed amid persistent suspected Russian gray-zone warfare against European NATO member states. On October 13, Bulgaria’s government summoned the Russian ambassador after two ships were hit by drones near its territorial waters.[REF] Two additional merchant ships were struck by drones near Bulgaria’s coast the week before, attacks that followed a strike on a civilian ship off Romania,[REF] and Romania has faced repeated Russian drone incursions over the past year.[REF]While not mentioning these and other similar events directly, General Grynkewich stated that threats and intimidation against Alliance members will only bind NATO closer together. He noted that this unity is enhanced by the Alliance’s confidence in its ability to move up the escalation ladder if needed. General Grynkewich identified NATO’s strength, cohesion, and readiness as notable factors that should significantly complicate an adversary’s military calculus of escalation. SACEUR also exhorted European NATO allies not to shy away from identifying the source of gray-zone provocations when they occur.The United States’ ongoing European force posture review and discussions of a likely reduction in U.S. troop levels in Europe as part of the necessary rebalancing of forces to the Indo-Pacific have led to uncertainty among NATO allies regarding America’s contributions to the Alliance.[REF] General Grynkewich’s speech reaffirmed the United States’ commitment to European security, albeit within the larger framework of increased burden sharing promoted by the Trump Administration.NATO’s theory of victory relies on aggressive, forward resistance to enemy advances. Implementing this operational concept will require the Alliance to bring substantial force to bear within a constrained timeline. While General Grynkewich’s speech serves as an overt commitment to a continued American presence in NATO, European states will likely have to shoulder a significant burden as part of the rapid joint response to an attack on the Alliance. To ensure NATO’s ability to execute this strategy, European states should continue expanding their defense spending to improve their warfighting capabilities, forward-deploy certain capabilities, and substantially improve military mobility.General Grynkewich prefaced his explanation of NATO’s theory of victory with a frank assessment of NATO’s security environment. He held that conflict is neither imminent nor inevitable. This status quo, he said, can be sustained by clearly articulating NATO’s intentions, maintaining open lines of communication with external states, and maintaining deterrence by denial through military capacity.Commenting on the character of NATO, General Grynkewich stressed that the Alliance is defensive and has “no plans, no intentions, and no ambitions” other than the protection of NATO peoples and territories. SACEUR nevertheless cautioned potential adversaries not to mistake NATO’s defensive nature for a lack of resolve and emphasized that member states will ensure any attack on Alliance territory will prove futile.[REF]This point was underlined by additional commentary regarding NATO’s deterrence posture. General Grynkewich drew attention to the Alliance’s “decision advantage.” He asserted that NATO will not be caught by surprise thanks to an immense intelligence footprint encompassing a vast network of sensors and sources. General Grynkewich framed NATO’s intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance capability as a key enabler of the Alliance’s theory of victory. By rapidly assessing an opposing force’s presence and intent, NATO forces will have time to mobilize in the numbers required to deny attackers at the point of contact, especially because these troops will be reinforcing significant numbers of NATO troops forward positioned within NATO’s easternmost states.Because of NATO’s doctrine, character, and posture, General Grynkewich remarked that the burden of escalation will always lie upon NATO’s aggressors. NATO’s Block, Blunt, Break strategy seeks only to prevent an enemy from realizing its revisionist aspirations. He plainly asserted that such states will “bear the full moral, political, and strategic weight” of initiating and expanding conflict with the Alliance.[REF]General Grynkewich included within this posture of deterrence and denial an explicit characterization of NATO’s intentions after the outbreak of conflict. He emphasized that the Alliance’s Block, Blunt, Break strategy does not seek at the outset to impose a strategic defeat upon its adversaries. Instead, NATO seeks simply to employ its theory of victory to maintain the Alliance’s territorial integrity by tactically defeating its attackers.In sum, General Grynkewich used his speech at the Warsaw Security Forum to communicate fundamental Alliance convictions to audiences both within and outside NATO. He articulated how NATO is not simply relying on decades-old defense strategies but adopting new means to meet emerging security threats. He delineated an internal Alliance dynamic defined by cohesion anchored in a collective determination to defend Alliance territory from opportunistic adversaries. He portrayed to external audiences a NATO whose mandate is limited to protecting its citizens and territory but that is also unified and firm in its willingness to fight and to defeat an aggressor if needed. General Grynkewich confidently messaged to Russia that he wants to assure those who “might be thinking about doing harm against us, that we’ve got this, and that they better not take any shot at the alliance.”[REF]Wilson Beaver is Senior Policy Advisor for Defense Budgeting and NATO Policy in the Allison Center for National Security at The Heritage Foundation.

This theory of victory is a marked shift from earlier NATO theories of victory, which focused on trading space for time—that is, allowing Russian forces to move into NATO territory, while NATO forces harass and slow Russian advances until decisive force can be brought to bear to destroy and then expel all Russian forces from NATO territory.

Block, Blunt, Break is a significant change from NATO Cold War strategy.

During the Cold War, West Germany was the NATO state considered most likely to be attacked by massive numbers of Soviet-led Warsaw Pact forces, and the Fulda Gap was often identified as the most likely attack route. The geographic size of West Germany meant that NATO forces could fall back tens or hundreds of kilometers before they could generate enough combat mass to begin a counteroffensive against Soviet and Warsaw Pact forces and then expel them from NATO soil. In this sense, NATO planned to trade territory for time, during which it would seize the conventional advantage.

It is not inconceivable that such a development could lead to the fracturing and potential breakup of NATO—long a goal of Moscow. This fresh strategy articulated by SACEUR could be a way to defend every inch of NATO soil from the outset and prevent this difficult scenario.

France: Sweeping Bill Threatens Peaceful Protest, Rights

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1229 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hrw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • (Paris, November 12, 2026) – A draft law that passed in its first reading by the French Senate on October 27, 2026, contains measures that would severely undermine the rights to peaceful assembly and freedom of expression, and are incompatible with France’s human rights treaty obligations, Human Rights Watch mentioned today.
  • Industry observers note that “Penalizing people engaged in their right to peaceful protest is the wrong answer to tackling violent disorder in France,” said Eva Cossé, senior Europe researcher at Human Rights Watch.
  • The bill was introduced by the government on September 16 under a fast-track procedure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Paris, November 12, 2026) – A draft law that passed in its first reading by the French Senate on October 27, 2026, contains measures that would severely undermine the rights to peaceful assembly and freedom of expression, and are incompatible with France’s human rights treaty obligations, Human Rights Watch mentioned today. The so-called “vandals pay” bill is now pending review by the National Assembly.

Industry observers note that “Penalizing people engaged in their right to peaceful protest is the wrong answer to tackling violent disorder in France,” said Eva Cossé, senior Europe researcher at Human Rights Watch. “Lawmakers in both houses should reject this problematic bill entirely.”.

The bill was introduced by the government on September 16 under a fast-track procedure. It was pushed forward and significantly toughened by opposition conservative senators in response to weeks of nationwide high school protests over what students see as the government’s under-investment in their education, and the violence that took place alongside school and cost-of-living protests on October 17 that included significant clashes with law enforcement and widespread looting and property damage across France. The bill builds on the momentum of legislation adopted in August to address serious public disorder, developed in response to concerns over illegal dance parties, football-related rioting, and racing vehicles on the streets.

While the purpose of the current legislation is ostensibly to address and deter violence and property damage, the text adopted by the Senate introduces measures that pose a serious threat to human rights, including the essence of the right to peaceful protest, Human Rights Watch said. The French authorities have also failed to put forward evidence that existing criminal justice measures are insufficient to address violent disorder or criminal damage.

The draft law provides for joint civil liability for property damage during a protest. It would allow courts to order individual participants, including the parents of children who participated, to pay up to €10,000 in damages—or perform community service—whether or not the individual committed acts of violence or caused the damage.

Sources indicate that people could be penalized simply for “knowingly” participating in an “unlawful assembly” (attroupement), defined in the French criminal code as “any gathering of people on a public highway or in a public place that is likely to disturb public order,” or for failing to disperse after the police glitch orders for a second time. Legal commentators have said that the requirement for prior dispersal orders is not an effective safeguard, because such orders are in practice either not issued or are not sufficiently audible.

Being present during a protest considered an unlawful assembly, or failing to leave the area fast enough following police orders to disperse, could trigger severe financial consequences. The bill requires prosecutors to share suspects’ identities with prefects, the interior minister’s local representative, and local authorities so they can pursue damage claims in civil court, even if the prosecutor has decided not to pursue criminal charges.

Recent findings suggest that the bill would allow criminal penalties of up to one year in prison and a €15,000 fine for organizers of banned protests, and six months in prison and a €7,500 fine for participants, or in some cases, a summary fine of €500 to avoid prosecution. Existing law allows six months in prison and a €7,500 fine only for protest organizers. Punishments can be doubled for people who cover their faces. The bill also gives prefects the power, without prior judicial oversight, to preemptively ban individuals from protests for 24 hours on the basis of police intelligence or evidence of repeated or serious violent behavior during the three preceding years.

Recent findings suggest that the bill broadens existing security and administrative measures that jeopardize rights, Human Rights Watch remarked. To recover court-ordered damages, after a conviction, the draft law allows the state to confiscate social security payments—child benefit, early-years child allowance, family supplement, family support allowance, back-to-school allowance, and solidarity allocation—from parents to pay for damages caused by their children under age 18. This measure risks disproportionally affecting low-income households.

It would also allow the authorities to deny social housing to adults convicted of “unlawful assembly” or serious public order offenses near residential buildings in the preceding three years, and to seek to evict families from social housing if a member of the household repeatedly engages in such acts.

The bill broadens existing powers under counterterrorism, child protection, and drug laws, that oblige tech companies, without a court order, to take down within 24 hours online content that authorities deem capable of provoking offenses, under the threat of blocking the site and massive fines.

The draft law extends the use of video surveillance to monitor public gatherings, and permits algorithmic processing to potentially identify protesters, measures first introduced for the Paris 2024 Olympics. Senators added a latest provision to authorize recording and transmitting footage from drones and other police aircraft to track, identify, and prosecute individuals for protest-related offenses, raising the prospect of general drone surveillance by police. Previous laws imposed stricter conditions on police drone deployments to monitor protests.

This draft law is part of a broader trend of erosion of the civic space and the rule of law in France, Human Rights Watch stated.

It has been revealed that the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the European Convention on Human Rights, to which France is a party, protect the rights to peaceful assembly and association and to freedom of expression. Although the treaties allow for restrictions on these rights, they must be subject to strict tests of necessity and proportionality.

In particular, the European Court of Human Rights has consistently emphasized that peaceful participants in a protest may not be held responsible for reprehensible acts committed by others, and that “this is true even when the demonstration results in damage or other disorder.” The court has previously found France violated this standard, ruling that even a lower end disciplinary sanction imposed on a protester who did not commit any culpable act, was not permitted. The court reminded France that in seeking to pursue a legitimate aim, the result must not to be to discourage people, for fear of sanctions, from being able to express their views including through peaceful protest.

According to recent reports, punishing individuals for the actions of others, and jailing and fining people simply for engaging in peaceful protest as a means of deterring violent disorder are not legitimate restrictions on those rights. The other measures in the bill also raise human rights concerns including in relation to the right to a fair trial, the right to privacy, and the rights to social security and housing.

In a recent development, “This bill is a human rights disaster,” Cossé remarked. “It undermines human rights that are central to a functioning democracy, punishes people for the actions of others and not only risks, but seems designed to deter, participation in peaceful protest.”.

This news release has been corrected to accurately reflect commentators’ concerns about the criminal code’s requirements for dispersing a protest.

  • Sources indicate that although the unfortunate Mr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A conversation with a student reminded me of one of my favorite articles, by my UCLA colleague Henry A. Kelly (who is emeritus in the English Department). It's called "Lawyers' Latin: Loquenda ut Vulgus?," and here's the introduction (though all 14 pages of the article are much worth reading):.

According to recent reports, in "Rex v. Venables and Others: The Dead Pronunciation" (one of A. P. Herbert's "Misleading Cases"), Mr. Wick, an advocate making his first appearance in the High Court, tries out his textbook Latin before the Lord Chief Justice. The young advocate, attempting to apply for a writ of certiorari, asks for "a rule of neesee of kairtiorahree." The Lord Chief Justice pretends not to understand this or any other of Mr. Wick's Latin phrases. When ultra vires is rendered ooltrah weerayze, the Court interrupts: "Stop! Listen, Mr. Wick. The two groups of sounds last formed by you have no meaning for me, and I order you not to make use of them again.".

Sources indicate that although the unfortunate Mr. Wick is genuinely baffled by the Court's pronunciation of Latin terms, he is offered scant sympathy:.

Industry observers note that it is not for me at my time of life to learn a newly introduced language; it is not for the King's judges to remodel their diction according to the whims of pedagogues or the habits of the Junior Bar. The bitter conclusion is, Mr. Wick, that you must go away and learn to pronounce the Latin tongue correctly, according to the immemorial practice of your profession.

Sources indicate that according to the juristic apophthegm, Loquendum ut vulgus, sentiendum ut docti, one should "speak like the common people but understand like the learned." When it comes to legal Latin, lawyers have observed the first part of this advice in various ways. Traditionally, Latin in England and other European countries has not been spoken uniformly but has been pronounced according to the sounds of the vernacular or lingua vulgaris of each region. Nowadays, however, most lawyers must be classed with the vulgus in never having learned Latin, and so they tend to avoid it whenever possible. But when an expression is unavoidable, they give it what they consider to be the "most common" pronunciation, or they imitate the commons in acting according to whim rather than according to rule. The result is what we might charitably call an eclectic or ad hoc approach—we hear, for example, ADD HOCK, ODD HAWK, ADD HOKE, ODD OAK, and so on.

Four different but internally consistent systems of Latin pronunciation have been used in England and America, each entirely "correct" and defensible in theory and in practice. The following analysis is concerned more with showing how the four methods have been adapted to English tongues than with reflecting how each would be spoken by a "native" or purist. My aim, after tracing the vagaries of Latin pronunciation, is to offer some practical recommendations to English-speaking lawyers using Latin phrases….

For the lawyer who occasionally uses Latin words or phrases, I recommend that all  expressions that have survived comfortably from an era when all Latin was pronounced in the English way—for example, et cetera—should continue to be pronounced as English, that is, in the English system of pronouncing Latin outlined above. But when Latin is cited as a foreign language, it should either be pronounced according to the system used by its author (if it is a literary citation) or according to any of the four systems outlined here that seems apt or convenient. Most often, no doubt, the system used will be the one learned in school.

But lawyers and legal educators should keep in mind the certainty of Herbert's Lord Chief Justice that such "hateful sounds" as "ooltrah weerayze" (for ultra vires) "will never proceed from the lips of an English judge, however many innocent boys are instructed to make them at school." Those who learned the Classical system need to be cautioned against trying to impose it upon all Latin expressions as if it were the only correct, or the most correct, way of pronouncing Latin. To do so would be to mistake the purpose of the scholars who resurrected it. It was intended only for the classics of the Golden Age of Latin, not for later Latin or for technical Latin terms or phrases brought into the various vernaculars in modern times.

According to recent reports, he labels the four methods "Classical (Ciceronian)," "Italian (Dantean)," "Continental (Chaucerian)," and "English (Shakespearean)," and discuss them further. He also cites a medieval source which I quite liked, at least with regard to pronunciation:.

[T]he desire to appear wise among the foolish … is itself a kind of madness.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

Creator and UGC content is only getting bigger as a growth channel for developer tools, and right now Supabase reaches it mostly at arm's length, through agencies that own the actual relationships with creators. This role exists to change that: bring our creator/influencer program fully in-house, own those relationships directly, and grow the program into a multi-million-dollar channel. A good marker of success looks like a roster of around 50 active creators within the first year — at which point we take what worked and go find the next channel to unlock the same way.

Recent findings suggest that this is a growth and marketing role first, not a DevRel or engineering-adjacent one — we're optimizing less for technical depth and more for someone outgoing enough that creators want to work with them directly, creative enough to keep testing new formats and strategies, and operationally strong enough to run the budgets and reporting behind it. The work is currently split on an interim basis across a couple of people on the marketing team; this role is being created to own it end to end.

Source, recruit, and manage direct relationships with content creators (TikTok, Instagram, YouTube).

Design and run creator campaigns end to end.

Find and test fresh acquisition channels and strategies — lots of small experiments, doubling down on what works.

Operationalize and report on these programs: budgets, tracking, results.

Grow with the role: the remit could develop into owning all content from a growth perspective, beyond creators and UGC.

3+ years in growth, partnerships or creator marketing at a dev tool, SaaS or consumer tech manufacturer.

Track record of launching channels from zero — and turning winners into repeatable programs.

Outgoing relationship-builder creators genuinely want to work with.

Strong operator. Comfortable with spreadsheets.

Ideally already doing a version of this somewhere scrappier or more startup — someone thriving at a smaller organization is a better signal here than someone comfortable (but not standout) at a big-name platform.

We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

It has been revealed that every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the manufacturer. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

According to recent reports, supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are vital to us.

Once a year, the entire company gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

According to recent reports, we operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

Industry observers note that supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

Recent findings suggest that we move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that on November 12, Hungary's Prime Minister Péter Magyar revealed that his government intends to ratify the Council of Europe Convention on preventing and combatting violence against women and domestic violence, also known as “Istanbul Convention,” as part of a comprehensive package of measures seeking to strengthen protection and dignity of women and girls. It is a welcome and timely step.

According to recent reports, in 2013, I interviewed 37-year-old Lívia from Budapest for Human Rights Watch’s report Unless Blood Flows which documented domestic violence in Hungary. She told me she had repeatedly called the police about her husband’s abuse and that the police even witnessed him beating her. Officers told her they could do nothing “unless blood flows.” Other women described similar responses, some telling me they had stopped calling for help.

The fresh government package would strengthen enforcement of restraining orders, make misuse of intimate images a distinct criminal offense, and provide special protections for victims and survivors of intimate partner violence in criminal proceedings.

According to recent reports, the government also plans to end the prescription requirement for emergency contraception and the requirement under the so-called “heartbeat decree” that forces women seeking abortions to listen to any embryonic or fetal cardiac activity. It also aims to help women and girls in need to access menstrual products. These measures are urgently needed and very welcome.

Industry observers note that parliament, then controlled by a two-thirds majority from the Fidesz/KDNP ruling coalition, blocked an earlier ratification effort in 2020. Ratification commits Hungary to binding standards on preventing violence, protecting victims and survivors including those without secure immigration status, and holding perpetrators accountable.

It has been revealed that alongside ratifying the convention, authorities should develop an implementation plan in consultation with victims, survivors and women’s rights organizations; Police should receive specialized training on intimate partner violence, how to assess risks and to act on credible threats, and how to work with the courts to enforce protection orders. And the government should adequately fund sufficient numbers of shelter spaces, legal aid, and counseling services nationwide. To ensure reforms are effective, authorities should collect and publish data on police responses and breaches of protection orders to facilitate assessment.

The real test of these reforms will be when a survivor like Lívia next calls the police for help. No one should have to bleed before police and authorities act.

  • According to their complaint, masked individuals from Columbia University's anti-Israel alliance, armed with hammers, knives, bolt cutters, chains, and zip ties, stormed Columbia's Hamilton Hall and confronted the two men.
  • In a recent development, assuming the allegations are true, this seems like an open and shut case under the KKK Act, which the Supreme Court has described as reaching organized mob violence directed at a protected group and those perceived as standing with it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Torres v. Carlson, currently pending before the Second Circuit, is a case brought by two Columbia University janitors under the Civil Rights Act of 1871 (KKK Act).

According to their complaint, masked individuals from Columbia University's anti-Israel alliance, armed with hammers, knives, bolt cutters, chains, and zip ties, stormed Columbia's Hamilton Hall and confronted the two men. The janitors' refusal to yield drew the ire of the rioters, who then assaulted them, detained them, and slurred them as Jew-lovers, Jew-workers, and Zionists. The rioters proceeded to seize the building, break windows to chain the doors shut, barricaded themselves inside, and unfurled banners declaring an "Intifada.".

In a recent development, assuming the allegations are true, this seems like an open and shut case under the KKK Act, which the Supreme Court has described as reaching organized mob violence directed at a protected group and those perceived as standing with it. See Carpenters v. Scott, 463 U.S. 825 (1983).

Nevertheless, the district court granted the defendants' motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim upon which relief could be granted. Covington & Burling has filed an amicus brief on behalf of Jon D. Michael of UCLA Law School, Matthew Segal of Tufts, with the Second Circuit, taking issue with the district court's decisions to:.

(1) resolve at the pleading stage questions of motive in the defendants' favor, crediting the defendants' characterization of their own motives over the plaintiffs' allegations and dismissing explicit antisemitic epithets as irrelevant;.

(2) treat supposed political motive as categorically negating discriminatory animus—disregarding both the mixed-motive framework that operates across federal antidiscrimination law and the settled principle that speech, even on political subjects, can evidence discriminatory intent; and,.

(3) view Jewish disagreement about whether all anti-Zionism is inherently antisemitic as dispositive proof that the specific anti-Zionist rhetoric in this case was not plausibly antisemitic—a standard that conflicts with binding precedent, contradicts how courts apply antidiscrimination law to groups other than Jews, and improperly gives any individual Jew the power to veto discrimination claims by all other Jews.

As an aside, there are several federal court decisions arising out of post-October 7 protest activity that strike many, including me, as applying stricter standards to civil rights plaintiffs claiming anti-Jewish violations of civil rights laws than precedent suggests applies to other plaintiffs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, (Beirut) – Emirati authorities have arbitrarily detained at least five Shia Muslim foreign residents since the United States and Israel carried out military strikes on Iran in February 2026, Human Rights Watch said today. The detentions appear to be based on the detainees’ religious identity.

According to recent reports, emirati authorities detained the residents, who had been in the UAE between 2 and 40 years, between March and May. They have not been brought before a judge or formally charged, three informed sources said.

“Emirati authorities appear to be rounding up residents simply based on their religious beliefs as Shia Muslims in a largely Sunni country rather than providing any evidence of wrongdoing, while trampling over people’s due process rights,” noted Joey Shea, senior UAE researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The authorities should immediately release anyone targeted because of their religion.”.

Sources indicate that between September and October, Human Rights Watch interviewed the three sources and reviewed CCTV footage of a raid on the company that one of the detainees owned. The detainees’ and sources’ names are withheld for fear of reprisals against them and their relatives.

The sources noted that security authorities asked at least one of the detainees about his religious affiliation before his arrest and interrogated at least one family member about their religious views. Another Shia community member warned at least one detainee and a relative to leave the UAE.

In a recent development, on March 23, Emirati state security arrested one man, 44, in Sharjah, as he was in his car near his home at midnight, a relative remarked. He was not allowed to contact a lawyer or his family that night.

The following night, Emirati security forces took the man to his family home for a search. The officers took money, jewelry, books, and credit cards, his relative remarked. Security forces did not inform him or his family of any charges against him.

The relative noted that a worker at the mosque they attended had warned him to leave the country in June 2025. The government “viewed us Shias as sleeper cells,” he said. The relative left the UAE two days later.

The same mosque worker asked the man on March 20, 2026, whether he had “any problems with the police.” The relative mentioned this was how the man had been warned, but he did not understand it as a warning and stayed in the UAE.

Emirati security forces also raided the man’s company. Human Rights Watch reviewed CCTV footage reportedly from the site, timestamped March 24. The footage shows two men, one in a baseball cap and the other in traditional clothing, entering the man’s company at around 9:19 p.m. and searching offices. One enters a room with computers and appears to tamper with the equipment.

In a recent development, the man was held in incommunicado detention for three days, then allowed to make a one-minute call to his family. He has been allowed two-minute calls every two weeks since. Prison authorities end the call if he attempts to reveal information about his case or location. His family has not been allowed to visit.

In a recent development, on September 14, the family learned through his lawyer that he had been moved to the notorious al-Sadr prison in Abu Dhabi, the source noted. Emirati authorities have held the prominent Emirati human rights defender Ahmed Mansour there since 2017 in conditions that may amount to torture.

On the evening of April 22, state security officials arrested a 38-year-old foreign Shia national at a money transfer office near his home in Sharjah, a relative stated. They took him to his home and searched it, seizing money, gold jewelry, and his laptop without informing his family of any charges.

It has been revealed that on May 29, Emirati authorities summoned his wife for questioning, including about her husband’s religious views, the source noted. Authorities released her at 10 a.m. on May 30.

Emirati authorities held him in incommunicado detention, allowing him to make a brief call on June 3, the source said. Authorities allow him one brief phone call every week in which he cannot reveal the details of his detention. The authorities told his wife on October 6 that he had been moved to al-Sadr prison. She has not been allowed to visit him.

Emirati authorities arrested three more foreign Shia nationals between April and May, a third source related to the men noted. Security forces raided the homes of all three men, confiscated their passports and money, and did not inform them of the charges against them, the source said.

According to recent reports, during one of the raids, a security officer asked a family member about their religion, job, and income, the source mentioned. Before the arrest, one of the men received a phone call from Emirati authorities asking about a religious problem and the names of his associates, the source said.

The three men have been allowed to make a brief call every ten days without revealing their location, the source said. Prison authorities end the call if they attempt to give details about the case or detention conditions.

“We all left the UAE in one day,” a family member said. “We wrapped up over 30 years in the UAE… We gave the UAE our hopes, dreams, and children. We sang their national anthem in schools. We loved this country.”.

Human Rights Watch has previously documented Emirati authorities arbitrarily detaining and forcibly disappearing and expelling other Shia residents, without due process, between 2009 and 2021. Reuters reported that thousands of Pakistani Shia residents have been deported from Gulf Arab states since February 28. During the same period, Emirati authorities revoked visas of Iranian families who have lived in the UAE for decades and banned Iranian nationals from transiting through the UAE, media and UAE Foreign Ministry reports remarked.

Industry observers note that on February 28, the United States and Israel carried out airstrikes on Iran, and Iran retaliated with strikes against Israel and Gulf states. Iran has since launched thousands of drones and missiles at Gulf countries, with the largest number striking the UAE. Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International found that Gulf governments responded by intensifying restrictions on the rights to freedom of expression, association, and peaceful assembly during the conflict, in an already repressive environment.

Industry observers note that under international law, governments have a responsibility to protect public safety in wartime, but security measures must be lawful, necessary, proportionate, and nondiscriminatory. Detaining people because of their religion and holding them without charge and access to lawyers is never justified, Human Rights Watch said.

“Emirati authorities should not treat the Shia community as a security threat in response to Iran’s unlawful strikes on the UAE,” Shea noted.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Between August 28 and September 16, US military forces intercepted and destroyed eight Ecuadorian fishing vessels, alleging that they served as floating refueling stations for drug-trafficking boats.
  • Since Human Rights Watch reported on the operations, Ecuadorian courts have acquitted 40 people.
  • The judge said the prosecution rested on a “chain of successive presumptions.” He admonished the prosecutor for pursuing an unsupported case and closed it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Between August 28 and September 16, US military forces intercepted and destroyed eight Ecuadorian fishing vessels, alleging that they served as floating refueling stations for drug-trafficking boats. They detained 146 of the 160 crew members and transferred them to Ecuadorian authorities, who charged 90 with “unlawful association.”.

Since Human Rights Watch reported on the operations, Ecuadorian courts have acquitted 40 people. In an October 29 judgment reviewed by Human Rights Watch, a Manta judge acquitted eight fishermen from a vessel named the Don Rufo. The prosecution’s own witnesses, including Ecuadorian police and Navy officials, testified that no illicit items were recovered, and that they knew of no prior investigation linking the fishermen to organized crime.

The judge said the prosecution rested on a “chain of successive presumptions.” He admonished the prosecutor for pursuing an unsupported case and closed it.

The ruling follows an October 7 decision acquitting another 32 crew members from the Conquista II and María Candelaria on similar grounds. The judge found no evidence supporting the unlawful association charge and admonished prosecutors for pursuing the case without even minimal evidence.

Industry observers note that out of the 160 crew members intercepted by the US, 110, that is 70 percent, are now free and without charges. Fourteen were not brought before Ecuadorian authorities, 56 were released without charge by a judge, and 40 were acquitted. Fifty others are awaiting trial.

Neither Ecuador nor the United States has publicly disclosed the operation’s legal basis, including the criteria used to intercept the vessels, and in some cases destroy them, or evidence linking the boats to drug trafficking.

Recent findings suggest that the US Congress should ensure oversight over these and other US security operations in and near Ecuador, where people have been detained without evidence and, in some cases, tortured by Ecuadorian personnel. Organized crime in Ecuador is a serious threat that should be addressed with an effective and rights respecting security and justice policy, not with human rights violations.

This article has been updated to reflect the correct number of crew members detained and overall intercepted by US military forces.

Scott Proctor. “No matter where they are in the world, the National Security Division of the Department of Justice will pursue those who target American citizens and American interests. Industry observers note that “As alleged, these defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members,” said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald for the Southern District of New York. “Even after one of their co-conspirators was arrested and placed in federal custody, the defendants allegedly continued coordinating terrorist activity through coded communications and a network of associates overseas. The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical — it is very real. Our Office will not stop working to address and disrupt this threat, and to prosecute those responsible.”.

According to the allegations contained in the superseding indictment and other court filings: Al-Saadi, Mohsen Mohajeri, and al-Hassani allegedly conspired to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the United States on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, which included the IRGC and Kata’ib Hizballah, both of which are FTOs. Most recently, in approximately September 2026, al-Hassani allegedly orchestrated a terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base (RAF Fairford) in Fairford, United Kingdom (the “RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot”), which at the time of the attempted attack, housed U.S. military aircraft and personnel.

Sources indicate that al-Hassani and Mohajeri, both of whom were in Iran at the time of the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot, allegedly relied on a network of contacts in the United Kingdom. Al-Saadi, who was imprisoned and awaiting trial on pending terrorism charges in the Southern District of New York, attempted to coordinate with al-Hassani and Mohajeri from jail by passing coded messages through third parties.

Al-Saadi, a longtime operative of the IRGC and Kata’ib Hizballah, was charged in May for working with and on behalf of the IRGC and Kata’ib Hizballah, as well as other FTOs, for his involvement in planning and promoting approximately 18 terrorist attacks in Europe; and for attempting to bomb a synagogue in New York. The picture below reveals al-Saadi in front of an array of machineguns in a conference room with a map of the United States on the wall next to a list of “legitimate targets” (redacted here) identifying former and current U.S. officials.

As alleged, among the individuals with whom al-Saadi worked to facilitate and carry out the European Terrorist Attacks were Mohajeri and al-Hassani. Mohajeri is an Iranian national and operative of the IRGC who coordinated with al-Saadi and al-Hassani to carry out those terrorist attacks with the IRGC’s backing. Al-Hassani, who is originally from Iraq, used his contacts and criminal associates to carry out terrorist attacks in the United Kingdom.

The European Terrorist Attacks were carried out in the name of a purportedly latest terrorist group with the pseudonym Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), which is a front for Kata’ib Hizballah and other FTOs. Of the 18 terrorist attacks in the spring of 2026 for which HAYI claimed responsibility in Europe, seven took place in the United Kingdom, the most of any European country. The attacks involved arsons, explosives, and in one instance, a near-fatal stabbing in London of two Jewish men, including a dual U.S.-British citizen.

In a recent development, al-Saadi, Mohajeri, and Al-Hassani were allegedly personally involved in planning many of the European Terrorist Attacks, and al-Saadi and Mohajeri helped create and publish online propaganda videos of these attacks. For example, on or about April 6, Mohajeri and al-Hassani planned attacks while together in a room in Iraq with a map of London displayed on a computer screen. In a video of that meeting, al-Hassani told Mohajeri, “we need to get focused on London.”  An image of the video is below, with Mohajeri on the right and al-Hassani on the left. HAYI then claimed responsibility for six terrorist attacks that occurred in and around London starting approximately one week later.

On or about April 17, al-Saadi, al-Hassani, and Mohajeri allegedly directed an individual to carry out one of the European Terrorist Attacks in real time. Specifically, al-Saadi, al-Hassani, and Mohajeri, along with others, were in a room watching a FaceTime video with the individual who was carrying out the attack, which was projected onto a large screen against the background of the HAYI logo. Al-Hassani directed the perpetrators’ actions, including by instructing the individual on the other end of the call to execute the attack and directing that individual to take a lighter and “light one in your hand,” “light it,” and “throw the fourth one.” Al-Saadi recorded the attack in real time, while Mohajeri recorded al-Hassani and al-Saadi in the room as they directed the attack. A still image from Mohajeri’s recording, showing al-Saadi (circled in red) and al-Hassani (circled in green), as they directed and filmed the attack, is below.

The next day, on or about April 18, al-Hassani participated in another video call with an individual carrying out an attack on a synagogue in London, with the HAYI logo projected on the background of al-Hassani’s screen. During the video call, al-Hassani directed the individual to “light it up like a Christmas tree.” The person on the video then lit an improvised explosive device and threw it at a building. An image from the video is shown below.

In March and April — overlapping with the time that al-Saadi was co-located in Iraq with Mohajeri and al-Hassani, planning the European Terrorist Attacks — al-Saadi allegedly attempted to coordinate and carry out terrorist attacks in the United States, including by targeting a synagogue in Manhattan.

Sources indicate that on or about May 1, following the European Terrorist Attacks, al-Saadi was arrested abroad and subsequently transferred to the custody of the United States to face prosecution. Al-Saadi has been in federal custody since his arrival in the United States. For approximately four months following al-Saadi’s arrest, there were no additional attacks attributable to al-Saadi, Mohajeri, and al-Hassani.

In August, however, al-Hassani allegedly directed and paid associates in the United Kingdom to conduct preparatory steps and arrange logistics for the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot. On Aug. 22, al-Hassani paid one individual (Individual-1) to perform pre-operational surveillance of RAF Fairford’s perimeter and al-Hassani subsequently received videos of the area surrounding the base. In later communications with al-Hassani, Individual-1 referred to him as “Ali.”.

According to recent reports, in September, al-Hassani also tasked and paid several individuals to help him prepare for the plot, including by procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching the purchase of chemical accelerants, including large quantities of potassium chloride, and purchasing metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel. At al-Hassani’s urging, those individuals commissioned custom decals that they affixed to the vans to create the appearance that they were used by a fuel delivery business and a swimming pool supply business.

On Sept. 26, al-Hassani allegedly tasked individuals to drive three vans, some of which were later determined to contain barrels of fuel, to the RAF Fairford base. That day, al-Hassani was in frequent communication with the van drivers, helping to coordinate their movements and directing them where to drive. At least two of the three vans, while en route to the perimeter of RAF Fairford, encountered a security roadblock and were not allowed to proceed on their intended route. Al-Hassani communicated with the drivers and occupants of the vans both before and after encountering the security checkpoint. In the early morning hours of Sept. 27, law enforcement authorities in the United Kingdom recovered three white vans to which the fuel delivery business logos were affixed and arrested the occupants.

While in prison in New York awaiting trial, al-Saadi has had phone calls with his immediate family members located in Iraq. As alleged, al-Saadi used those calls to pass coded messages to Mohajeri and al-Hassani in the days leading up to the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot.

Recent findings suggest that for example, in June and July, al-Saadi allegedly spoke with his mother and sister about Mohajeri. During those calls, they referred to Mohajeri by various aliases, including “Abbas, Abu Daniel” and “Sayyid Abbas.”  Al-Saadi also told his family members that he owed money to Mohajeri and directed them to pass along messages to Mohajeri about “work,” a term al-Saadi regularly used to describe terrorist activity, including on social media posts and in discussions with Mohajeri about partnering to conduct terrorist attacks. On one of those calls, al-Saadi also asked his sister, “What are they doing about all our old work?” and asked her whether it had been cancelled or just put on pause. Al-Saadi’s sister responded that “it isn’t cancelled.”.

On or about Sept. 24, al-Saadi once again spoke with his immediate family by phone. On the call, al-Saadi allegedly inquired about how al-Hassani, whom al-Saadi referred to as “Ali,” was doing. Al-Saadi’s family informed al-Saadi that “Ali” had been transferred to the “International Section.”  Al-Saadi then allegedly instructed his family to “give him [al-Hassani] money so we can do it.”  As described above, three days later, al-Hassani orchestrated the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot.

According to recent reports, al-Saadi, 32, is a citizen of Iraq and Iran. Mohajeri, 48, is a citizen of Iran. Al-Hassani, 35, is a citizen of Iraq. A chart containing the names, charges, and minimum and maximum penalties for the defendants is set forth below.

According to recent reports, the Justice Department praised the outstanding investigative work of the FBI’s New York Joint Terrorism Task Force, which consists of investigators and analysts from the FBI, the NYPD, and over 50 other federal, state, and local agencies, and the FBI Washington Field Office, Counterterrorism Division, as well as the assistance of the Department of Justice’s National Security Division, Counterterrorism Section, the Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs, U.S. Customs and Border Protection, the NYPD, the New York State Police, and the Department of State.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Jeffrey W. Coyle, Sarah L. Kushner, David J. Robles, and Chelsea L. Scism for the Southern District of New York are prosecuting the case, with assistance from James Donnelly and Paul Casey of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section.

A superseding indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

#44044. No Pseudonymity for Woman Alleging She Was Falsely Accused of Sexual Relationship with Jeffrey Epstein, Doxed
