    A Tribute to Judge Posner, from Vice Chief Judge David Weinzweig (Ariz. Ct. App.)

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (804 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I thought I'd pass along this tribute, which I thought was moving and apt:.
    • Twenty years ago, I was elevated to chair the antitrust section of the State Bar of Arizona, and I needed a headliner to pack the room for my first event.
    • So I cold-emailed Judge Posner an invitation to address judges, lawyers and law students in Tempe.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I thought I'd pass along this tribute, which I thought was moving and apt:.

    Dinner with Judge Richard Posner.

    Twenty years ago, I was elevated to chair the antitrust section of the State Bar of Arizona, and I needed a headliner to pack the room for my first event. Who in the world of antitrust could draw interest outside that world? The answer was obvious: the closest thing antitrust has to a rock star, Judge Richard Posner.

    So I cold-emailed Judge Posner an invitation to address judges, lawyers and law students in Tempe. I doubted he would reply, but he did, swiftly. He would be happy to come—under one condition. I told him to name it.

    Industry observers note that no antitrust law. Anything but antitrust law.

    I agreed, of course. He could have lectured on gardening for all I cared.

    Sources indicate that we all have our favorite jurists, past and present. Until last week, Judge Posner was my favorite living one. He died at 87. His writing is the reason I became an antitrust lawyer.

    Thirty years in the law, and I still turn to one trusted source when an problem is opaque or abstract. I run a quick Westlaw search for Judge Posner's take, and the fog lifts.

    Industry observers note that judge Posner wrote more than 3,300 judicial opinions, and he wrote them to be understood. He embodied what Judge Learned Hand preached nearly a century ago: "The language of law must not be foreign to the ears of those who are to obey it." Posner wrote for the people.

    He turned abstract ideas into concrete images. Consider his advice to lawyers who ignored the law that cut against them: "The ostrich is a noble animal, but not a proper model for an appellate advocate." I'm not endorsing the tone, but the point slugs you in the jaw.

    According to recent reports, posner made hard things look easy, and he worked hard at it. He confessed to going through up to 20 drafts to give his opinions "a casual, colloquial, and spontaneous appearance." As he put it, "I admit to hypocrisy in working so hard to give the appearance of effortlessness!".

    Recent findings suggest that judge Posner kept his promise and came to Arizona to speak on judicial independence, not antitrust. That night I hosted him for dinner at El Chorro, nestled at the base of Camelback and Mummy mountains.

    It has been revealed that I was scared. What would I say to Richard Posner for two hours? Convinced I could not carry the conversation alone, I recruited reinforcements, including the Chief Justice of the Arizona Supreme Court and a neurosurgeon.

    I opened with a safe question. Had anyone seen any good movies lately?

    According to recent reports, posner went first. The last movie he had seen in a theater was Superman. In 1978. Of course. Of course that was the last movie he saw. He did not have time for those trifling pursuits.

    It has been revealed that but then he leaned in. He and his wife had recently bought the first three seasons of 24 on DVD. Each episode, he marveled, captured one hour in a single day in the life of the protagonist, a man named Jack Bauer. A clock even appeared in the lower left-hand corner of the screen so viewers could watch the minutes tick by in real time. Posner narrated his favorite scenes as Bauer landed in one jam after another and always found a way out.

    Recent findings suggest that I have told that story to my law clerks for years. Posner described 24 with the passion and precision he brought to his opinions.

    Posner was an independent thinker who questioned what everyone else assumed, including his own views. He was a founder of the law and economics movement, building much of it with his longtime friend and collaborator, the economist William Landes.

    Posner moved antitrust from the boardroom to the checkout line. He asked whether the alleged anticompetitive conduct created efficiencies and raised or lowered prices for consumers. Courts had not always asked. The Chicago School has largely guided courts and regulators since the Reagan years.

    Sources indicate that I wrote one book. Posner wrote more than 50, ranging from Law and Literature to Reflections on Judging, all while carrying a full caseload. A 2000 study by Fred Shapiro ranked him the most cited legal scholar of the second half of the twentieth century.

    Posner's opinions will lift the fog for generations of advocates. A reporter once asked him how law schools could improve legal writing. He said he would have first-year students read Holmes, Learned Hand and Robert Jackson, then try to write with their clarity. Posner is on that list. Law schools should teach his writing.

    Elly Griffiths’ 5 favorite female detectives in fiction

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1132 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I’m sure Eve knew immediately who killed Abel, although admittedly there was only one suspect.
    • It was some time, though, before crime-solving women appeared in print.
    • Recent findings suggest that interestingly, these first women sleuths were professionals, in that they earned their living from detection.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Women have always solved crimes. I’m sure Eve knew immediately who killed Abel, although admittedly there was only one suspect. Grendel’s mother, in Beowulf, is one of the greatest justice-seekers in literature. The Wife of Bath would make a formidable sleuth, specializing in domestic cases.

    It was some time, though, before crime-solving women appeared in print. In The Female Detective by Andrew Forrester (the pseudonym of James Redding Ware), published in 1864, Mrs Gladden is thought to be a dressmaker but is, in fact, a detective. The Revelations of a Lady Detective by William Hayward, also published in 1864, features Mrs Paschall, recruited by the Chief of Police to form a squad of women officers. In Mr Bazalgette’s Agent by Leonard Merrick, published in 1888, Miriam Lea is an aristocrat who becomes a private eye after falling on hard times.

    Recent findings suggest that interestingly, these first women sleuths were professionals, in that they earned their living from detection. The era of the talented but overlooked amateur, exemplified by Miss Marple, comes later.

    Sources indicate that when I created forensic archaeologist Dr Ruth Galloway, I was drawing on the tradition of the civilian expert, often a woman, who assists the police. There many great unofficial detectives in modern crime fiction;  Freida Klein in Nicki French’s books, for example, or Rhona Macleod in Lin Anderson’s series. There are also many terrific women police officers: Val McDermid’s Karen Pirie, Sarah Hilary’s Marnie Rome, Nadine Matheson’s Anjelica Henley,  Jane Casey’s Maeve Kerrigan.

    Here are five of my favorite female detectives, official or otherwise.

    Industry observers note that she’s not, strictly speaking, a detective but Marian Halcombe in The Woman in White by Wilkie Collins, is surely one of the greatest sleuths in crime fiction. Laura Fairlie is ostensibly the heroine but Marian, clever, brave and intrepid, is the beating heart of the book.

    It has been revealed that the Woman in White, published in 1859/60, is known as one of the great “sensation novels” and the sweeping narrative includes abduction, organized crime and murder. One of the most thrilling scenes has Marian clambering over rooftops at night in order to overhear a conversation between the villains Percival Glyde and Count Fosco. She’s in her petticoat because her voluminous silk skirt would have rustled too much. No wonder even evil Fosco is more than half in love with her.

    No list would be complete without Agatha Christie’s famous spinster sleuth. Jane Marple was apparently inspired by the many unmarried women after the first world war, who, as they grew older, were often ignored by the world around them.

    Sources indicate that miss Marple, poised with rose clippers in her garden or bent over her crochet, makes the most of her invisibility. Almost every crime reminds Miss Marple of something she saw in her home village of St Mary Mead. She’s caustic, quietly brilliant and ruthless when on the trail of a murderer. In A Caribbean Mystery Jason Rafiel describes her as “Nemesis in a pink shawl.” Miss Marple is also surprisingly well-travelled, helped by a generous nephew and a doctor who is always happy to prescribe a holiday.

    According to recent reports, I was delighted to be asked to contribute to Marple, a new collection of short stories featuring the divine Miss M. It was a daunting task made easier by the fact that we all think we know Miss Marple but she can still always surprise us.

    Ann Cleeves meant The Crow Trap to be a standalone novel. She was as surprised as anyone when, after a death at an isolated cottage in the Pennines, a rather unusual detective arrives to solve the case.

    Sources indicate that DI Vera Stanhope is “a large woman, amply covered” with a bulbous nose, man-sized feet and pitted skin. She’s scruffily dressed and carries a plastic bag containing her notes. She’s also brilliant, unconventional and frighteningly forthright. There are now thirteen Vera novels with a fourteenth, rumored to be the last, scheduled for 2027.

    The TV series Vera, starring Brenda Blethyn as the eponymous detective, has run for fourteen seasons. Through the years we have learnt more about Vera’s history and her deep connection to the Northumbrian countryside but we can never second-guess our heroine who, like the similarly disheveled Columbo, always has the last word.

    Sources indicate that nancy Spain wrote six fantastically funny and atmospheric crime novels starring the indomitable Miriam Birdseye. I’m sure she would have gone on to write more if she hadn’t been killed in a  plane crash at the untimely age of forty-six. But in Miriam, Nancy has given us a detective for all time.

    Industry observers note that miriam is a  wildly glamorous “vaudeville star” whose modus operandi seems to be to get engaged to the prime suspect as promptly as possible. Miriam’s sidekick is the Russian ballerina, Natasha Nevkorina, whose ambition is to do as little as possible. Miriam is always prepared to dress up in the name of detection. Was there ever a better chapter heading than this, in Cinderella Goes to the Morgue–Enter Miriam, Disguised as a Principal Boy?

    It has been revealed that susie Steiner also left us tragically early, dying of a brain tumor in 2022. She only wrote three novels featuring DS Manon Bradshaw but she created one of my favorite modern detectives.

    Recent findings suggest that manon, named after the operatic heroine, is a terrific character: clever, kind, funny and often frustratingly stubborn. Manon’s relationships with her colleagues, Davy and Harriet, and, especially, with her adopted son, Fly, are beautifully described; full of warmth, nuance and humour. I’m sorry that there aren’t more novels about Manon, but this trilogy is crime-writing perfection.

    Stella Darnell first appears in The Detective’s Daughter by Lesley Thomson. Stella is the daughter of a police officer who died before he could solve his most important case. Stella had a complicated relationship with her father and has taken another path; she’s a cleaner.

    It has been revealed that through the course of ten intricately-plotted books, Lesley Thomson charts how Stella, reluctantly at first, becomes a private detective whilst running her own cleaning agency. She solves crimes “stain by stain.” Along the way, Stella acquires a wonderful collection of assistants, including Jack Harmon, a tube driver who can sense murder….

    According to recent reports, elly Griffiths is the author of the Ruth Galloway and Brighton mystery series, as well as the standalone novels The Stranger Diaries, winner of the Edgar Award for Best Novel; The Postscript Murders; and Bleeding Heart Yard. She is the recipient of the CWA Dagger in the Library Award and the Mary Higgins Clark Award. She lives in Brighton, England.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that we all have a picture in our head of a mother—what we think a mother should be or shouldn’t be, what ideal motherhood looks like. Society creates expectations for mothers, and mothers who color outside those lines are often censured by those around them.

    Sources indicate that but being a mother, or a stepmother, or a mother figure, is hard. If you carry a child you might think that pregnancy will be nine months of glowing, radiant bliss (that’s what all those parenting influencers say on TikTok, don’t they?) Instead, you’re coping with swollen feet and sciatica, and the constant worry that you might do something that will accidentally harm your growing baby.

    In a recent development, once your child is born you might think, Great, it’s going to be nothing but sunshine and roses from here on out. But parenting isn’t just drippy ice cream cones on the beach and smiling while riding carousels. There are so many things you can’t anticipate—unexpected illnesses, trouble at school, headstrong kids who simply want their own way.

    The truth of the matter that having a child and raising a child are often some of the most anxiety-riddled years of a person’s life. Even when nothing’s going wrong, a mother can often feel like something just might go wrong. The worry they are feeling is somehow a hedge against bad things happening—parental anxiety as a shield against actual harm.

    It has been revealed that fictional mothers, of course, get the worst of it. It’s bad enough that real-world mothers have to cope with spiking fevers and school permission forms and judgmental in-laws. But what if you desperately want a child but it turns out your baby was also, say, the son of Satan? Or what if you love your children with all your heart but you keep hearing things, seeing things that you aren’t sure are actually there? What if the people around you aren’t to be trusted? What if you feel like you can’t trust yourself?

    Everyone knows about Rosemary, right? Poor Rosemary Woodhouse, whose gaslighting jerk of a husband, Guy, trades her womb for a successful career.

    In Ira Levin’s classic novel of motherhood horror, Rosemary’s Baby, Rosemary is a cheery newlywed who wants to have a child. Guy is a struggling actor who keeps just missing his big break and wants to wait a little longer to start a family. A bit of timely luck allows them to sign a lease in an older building called the Bramford, a place that’s notoriously difficult to get into. Rosemary is thrilled that, at least, she will have the decoration of a new place to keep her busy, but she still wishes for a baby.

    Sources indicate that an older couple, Roman and Minnie Castavet, live in the next apartment. Rosemary finds them nosy and annoying, but for some reason Guy likes them and starts to visit regularly. Then, a miracle happens. The actor who cast in a role that Guy almost got is suddenly struck blind (a miracle for Guy, of course, not so much for the other actor) and Guy lands a role that can make his career. Soon after this unexpectedly fortuitous occurrence, he decides that he does, in fact, want a baby.

    Industry observers note that shortly after, Rosemary has a terrible dream—a dream about a beast who rapes her while several people look on. And then, the second miracle happens. Rosemary is pregnant. Except her pregnancy doesn’t feel right, and everyone around her keeps telling her it’s fine.

    Rosemary’s journey is so harrowing because no matter what she says or does or even knows with absolute certainty, no one will believe her. If you’ve never read this one it’s time to give it a try.

    Kit Burgoyne’s The Captive is a clever play on the I’ve-been-impregnated-by-Satan-against-my-will story, or in this case, by an entity alternately referred to as “The Long-Before” or “Him.” An underground revolutionary group that call themselves the Nail decide to kidnap Adeline Woolsaw, the wealthy heiress of a vast network of connected businesses, in hopes of exposing the Woolsaws and their corruption to the public. The only time Adeline ever seems to leave the vast estate where she lives is to go to the doctor’s office, so the group decides to grab her as she leaves her appointment.

    Unfortunately for the Nail, Adeline is pregnant. Even more unfortunately, Adeline is going into labor in the van. Just to add to their confusion, Adeline most definitely does not want to return home to her parents. It seems that her parents worship this evil entity and arranged to have Adeline carry His child in order to establish total world domination.

    This pitch-black story skewers the cultists, the radical revolutionaries and the oligarchs that run everything equally and mashes it all up into a super-fun (and frequently gory) thriller.

    Helen Phillip’s The Need is probably one of my favorite novels of the last ten years. I’ve never read another book that so accurately embodies both the intense love of a mother for her children and also the profound, dragging monotony of the daily tasks that make up her day.

    Molly is a mom of two and a paleobotanist, alone with the kids while her partner travels. She is exhausted, exhausted in that bone-deep way parents often are, feeling like she wants to stay on top of everything but she simply cannot.

    When she hears footsteps in her home she thinks she’s imagining them. She’s anxious about a potential home invasion. She can’t trust herself. She’s just sleep-deprived. But then she comes face to face with an intruder wearing a mask, and the reality of Molly’s world tilts precariously on its side.

    It has been revealed that the less you know about this one, the better. It unfolds like a strange and fascinating puzzle box, revealing layers as it goes.

    Sources indicate that neena Viel’s debut Listen to Your Sister isn’t about a mother, per se. But it is about Calla Williams, a twenty-five-year-old woman just trying to keep it together, who reluctantly agrees to become the guardian to her sixteen-year-old brother Jamie. Jamie, like most 16-year-olds, is not interested in his sister’s authority, or any kind of authority, really. Their brother Dre agreed to help Calla with Jamie, but he has his own struggles and isn’t exactly present.

    Recent findings suggest that calla keeps trying, keeps sacrificing, keeps muddling along trying to do her best like every mother figure. Ever since her brothers were young she’s had visions of their dying in horrible ways, and her nightmares stoke her anxiety over their well-being. But her resentment is growing. No matter how much she loves her brothers, they don’t seem to love her enough to change.

    Recent findings suggest that one day Jamie’s behavior goes a little too far and the siblings are forced to flee their homes to hide out at a cabin in the woods. It’s there that Calla’s patience finally snaps, and her brothers discover that the nightmares Calla has had all their lives might just be real.

    Sources indicate that neena Viel’s writing is so intense, so profoundly visual, that this book has been indelibly imprinted on my brain. I’m still thinking about it months later.

    In my own upcoming novel Pinfeathers, stay-at-home mom Nora Pacetti is tired and frustrated that her husband, Adam, isn’t keeping up his end of the parenting bargain. But those problems seem trivial once Nora discovers a strange object sticking out of her baby’s arm.

    Nora thinks it must be a splinter. But when she examines it closely the object seems to have come through her daughter’s skin, not pierced it from the outside. Then Nora’s mother Giulia looks at it and renders her verdict—it’s a pinfeather, a baby feather.

    Nora doesn’t know what to believe, and then she finds another one. Does her daughter have a strange disease, or is she actually turning into a bird?

    Christina Henry is the author of The Mermaid, Lost Boy, Alice, Red Queen, and the national bestselling Black Wings series featuring Agent of Death Madeline Black and her popcorn-loving gargoyle, Beezle.

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1085 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    5 Books About Small Town Crime, from ‘Baby Queen’ Author Ty Landers

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1085 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, you expect danger in the city.
    • Sources indicate that there’s plenty of menace in small places.
    • I write crime thrillers set in places where people only recently started locking their doors.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, you expect danger in the city. Adjectives like streetwise and street-smart exist to acknowledge the specific intelligence needed to navigate the perils of urban living. Country intelligence has no succinct adjectives. Country-strong, that’s a thing. But, country-wise? More often than not, there is a misconception that life in the hinterlands will dull your edge, diminish your reflexes, lull you into a false sense of security.

    Sources indicate that there’s plenty of menace in small places. In towns with no interstate ramp, nameless desert stops with no cell phone service, a desperate farm community surrounded by an ocean of corn.

    I write crime thrillers set in places where people only recently started locking their doors. These don’t have to be set in the South—mine are—but they can happen anywhere. Maybe it’s Southern noir when done south of the Mason-Dixon line. Rural noir is a good name, and throws its arms around the whole genre, but it’s a mouthful. It comes out sounding slurry, even when I’m sober, and might not come out at all if I’ve had a cocktail. This subgenre of crime fiction goes by many names. I wish I could just tell people I wrote Southerns and have them understand—the way most people understand the Western. Till then, here are five of my favorite examples of novels that take place out past the last lights of town.

    Important note: I had to leave out a lot of authors I adore and beg you to read anything and everything by the following for outstanding examples of small-town, insular, tight-nit, and Sun-Belt crime: Flannery O’Connor, S.A. Cosby, Carson McCullers, Henry Wise, Attica Locke, Dennis Lehane, Megan Abbott, Ivy Pochoda, and Elmore Leonard. Please find them.

    Sources indicate that daniel Woodrell is incredible. I love every word he has ever written but Tomato Red is my favorite. It opens with a gorgeous run-on sentence that’s almost three hundred words long and, after reading it, it’s almost impossible not to collapse and read the whole book in one sitting. The novel’s hapless anti-hero, Sammy Barlach—recently fired from a dog food factory and fresh off a speed-fueled burglary attempt—throws in with siblings Jason and Jamalee Merridew. Jason, a local object of female obsession, and his sister Jamalee want to weaponize Jason’s beauty, blackmail wealthy woman, and get them both out of Venus Holler. Sammy hitches his wagon to the Merridew’s scheme. But for Jason, a gay man in the hills and hollows of the Ozarks, choosing to live an authentic life proves to me more dangerous than one of crime.

    According to recent reports, one of my favorite sayings from Tod Goldberg is that he writes about bad people doing terrible things to even worse people. In The Low Desert, he demonstrates this across twelve sometimes-connected stories set on the outskirts of California and Nevada. There are lonely deserts, fading resort towns, lost highways. Each story is a banger, but the fact that Goon Number Four isn’t your favorite TV show of the last decade is a miscarriage of justice. A story about a hired gun who enrolls in a community college, seeking to be rid of the life, only to find exploitation waiting in the halls of normalcy. The Low Desert has something I have never been able to fully articulate—feeling more like a great album, than the seminal work of crime fiction it is.

    Recent findings suggest that A personal favorite, Thompson’s Pop. 1280 is a novel that perfectly balances menace and comedy. Nick Corey, a terrible sheriff, oversees the 1280 souls of Potts County, Texas. Many of Nick’s constituents don’t want a sheriff, prefer to skirt the law, and tolerate him because he is pathologically shiftless. Our sheriff eats five meals a day, sleeps with any woman who’s up for it, sees murder as the only option rather than a last resort, and will do anything to keep his job. Not because he is ambitious, but because being sheriff allows him to do almost nothing. But, on the precipice of a difficult reelection, he reluctantly springs into action. Through the ensuing morass, Nick confronts sassy pimps, his pushy wife and her brother, his mistress and her husband, the town as whole, and the very concept of righteousness. Corey is a man who seems dumb, but isn’t. Someone dangerous and ruthless in the most peculiar and befuddling ways.

    Cormac McCarthy, No Country for Old Men.

    According to recent reports, cormac McCarthy’s most accessible novel. It is a literary crime novel that dissects the corrosive effects of money, heightened to break-neck entertainment by the inclusion of one of fiction’s most unforgettable bad dudes. In many ways, this is Anton Chigurh’s book the way Jaws belongs to the shark. Chigurh, a relentless hitman who’s as dangerous to his employers as he is to his targets, is evil with biblical scope. Ed-Tom Bell is a good man fading. A sheriff having and existential crisis, struggling to adapt to the requirements of his calling in a world where criminality has moved past opportunism and into something inconceivable. Throw in Llewelyn Moss, a Vietnam vet who stumbles across two million dollars after a drug deal goes wrong, and you’re in for a ride. When Chigurh’s tide of malevolence come in. One man tries to stem it, the other retreats. Fates are decided by the flip of a coin.

    Frank Bill, Crimes in Southern Indiana.

    According to recent reports, frank Bill’s debut, Crimes in Southern Indiana, is a cold look at a brutal version of Indiana that exists off the interstates. Southern Indiana is an anomaly—not quite the South, not quite the Midwest. Claimed by none—like the folks Bill writes about. He drops seventeen stories about this distinct region across two hundred and seventy pages in an achingly authentic voice. He can do more damage in ten pages than most other savvy word-geeks could with a lifetime supply of paper. The Penance of Scoot McCutchen will wreck you. I think about it all the time.

    Ty Landers holds an MFA in Creative Writing and Writing for the Performing Arts from the University of California, Riverside. Born and raised in Alabama, he spent more than twenty years in Nashville, Tennessee, before moving to Milwaukee, Wisconsin, with his wife and sons. His debut novel BABY QUEEN, out on November 17, 2026, is being adapted by HBO. For more on Ty Landers, visit: https://www.tylandersfiction.com/.

    Industry observers note that A federal judge sentenced Deontae Jackson, 37, of Minneapolis to 10 years in prison for his role in a Racketeering Influenced Corrupt Organization (RICO) conspiracy that included violence and fentanyl distribution. Jackson is the first of 14 defendants sentenced in this case, U.S. v. Alowonle et al. (24-cr-293).

    According to court documents, beginning on or about 2009 and continuing through at least April 2026, Jackson was a member of and associated with the Lows gang. The Lows gang does not have a formal structure or initiation process as it is comprised of several affiliated subsets. Members would prove their loyalty by “putting in work,” which included committing acts of violence and drug trafficking.

    Industry observers note that between February 2023 and May 2024, Jackson sold fentanyl as part of, and to benefit, the Lows gang. The Lows drug trafficking activities during this period involved over 1.2 kilograms of fentanyl.

    In a recent development, on April 26, 2024, law enforcement searched a home in Fridley, Minnesota, where Jackson was staying. In Jackson’s bedroom, officers found approximately 945 M-30 fentanyl pills, which collectively weighed around 94.5 grams. At the time of the search, Jackson was on electronic court monitoring in connection with his conviction for a gang-related drive-by shooting. After the search, Jackson removed his ankle monitor to avoid having his location tracked.

    Sources indicate that in May 2024, law enforcement tracked Jackson to Bismarck, North Dakota. Officers then searched Jackson’s hotel room where he was staying with a fellow Lows member and two others. Police recovered a bag containing 2,599 M-30 fentanyl pills that weighed approximately 270.4 grams. In a second bag, officers found 20 more M-30 fentanyl pills that weighed 2.08 grams.

    According to recent reports, assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division; Special Agent in Charge Joseph Persails of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) St. Paul Field Division; Special Agent in Charge Christopher D. Dotson of the FBI Minneapolis Field Office; Acting Special Agent in Charge Rafael Mattei of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) Omaha Field Division; Acting Special Agent in Charge Robert J. Kuszynski of the IRS Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI) Chicago Field Office; Special Agent in Charge Travis Pickard of the Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) St. Paul Field Office; and Inspector in Charge Brian Musgrove of the U.S. Postal Inspection Service (USPIS) Denver Division made the announcement.

    #43986. Chuck Thompson on the mysterious deaths of two Bigfoot hunters in Washington

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (993 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Chuck Thompson on the mysterious deaths of two Bigfoot hunters in Washington

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (993 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, skamania county rarely, if ever, captures the attention of the national news media.
    • On Christmas morning 2024, two men from Portland, Oregon, were reported missing in the wilds of Washington state.
    • “Two Portland men searching for Sasquatch and missing since early Christmas morning were found dead in the Gifford Pinchot National Forest—likely from exposure and being ill prepared,” the station reported.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, skamania county rarely, if ever, captures the attention of the national news media. Let alone the international news media. But during the traditionally slow Christmas holiday, when even serious outlets stoop to tracking Santa’s progress across the northern hemisphere and presenting expert commentary on decorations at the White House, the story about the bodies found in the backwoods of the Pacific Northwest arrived like a Christmas gift from News Kringle.

    On Christmas morning 2024, two men from Portland, Oregon, were reported missing in the wilds of Washington state. After a three-day search that involved more than sixty volunteers from two states, dogs, drones, and helicopters working through harsh terrain, icy conditions, and a snowstorm, their frozen bodies were recovered. On December 28, Portland’s CBS television affiliate KOIN 6 was among the first to pick up the story.

    “Two Portland men searching for Sasquatch and missing since early Christmas morning were found dead in the Gifford Pinchot National Forest—likely from exposure and being ill prepared,” the station reported.

    Recent findings suggest that did someone say Sasquatch? Every editor in the world knew clickbait when they saw it. Within days, near-identical headlines appeared around the world, backed by the biggest names in news.

    CNN: 2 Oregon men die from exposure in a forest after they went out to look for Sasquatch.

    Fox News: 2 dead after search for Sasquatch in Washington national forest.

    NPR: 2 men were found dead from exposure after looking for Sasquatch.

    BBC: Two men found dead while searching for Bigfoot.

    Nine News Australia: Two men found dead in US after going on Christmas Eve hunt for Bigfoot.

    Recent findings suggest that hundreds, perhaps thousands, jumped in. The Associated Press. MSN. CBS News. HuffPost. Newsweek. Today. Yahoo News. USA Today. Latest York Post. Los Angeles Times. San Francisco Chronicle. The Times. Daily Mail.

    The story was such a surefire traffic pusher that even specialized outlets ran with it. People. Sports Illustrated. AccuWeather. The celebrity and entertainment website TooFab. Spain’s national sports tabloid Marca. Latest Zealand’s Stuff. Taiwanese tabloid CTWant. The massively popular 52hrtt, a Chinese-language website that serves the global Chinese diaspora.

    There was no video, so each outlet looped the same images from a package of photos released by the Skamania County 23 sasquatch country Sheriff’s Office: four SAR volunteers on a snow-covered trail carrying an extension ladder through the forest; six volunteers in safety-orange jackets and helmets, one pointing a finger into the woods, using an extension ladder laid on the ground to cross a stream; a guy on hands and knees crawling across the ladder over a stream; a group of seven searchers using downed logs to cross a stream; and a Coast Guard helicopter hovering above an opening in the forest canopy.

    According to recent reports, in a digitally powered echo chamber, local, regional, national, and international outlets repeated the story almost word for word. All the way across the continent, News Center Maine television led its December 30 national news roundup in typical fashion:.

    We’ll start in Washington state. Two men were found dead there after going on a search for Bigfoot. They went out on their search a few days before Christmas Eve. When they didn’t return, family members contacted police. They were found after a three-day search. Local authorities there say it seems as though they likely died of exposure because of the weather conditions at the time and not being prepared.

    Sasquatch hunters. Christmas search. Poorly prepared. Died of exposure. That was all anyone seemed to know.

    In a recent development, in fact, those elementary pieces of the story were all anyone in the news media actually did know. As even a cursory examination of the torrent of articles and broadcasts about the two bodies found in the forest demonstrated, the stories were noteworthy mostly for their striking uniformity and lack of information. But something about the story wasn’t right. Something didn’t add up.

    According to recent reports, the rule that credible journalists are meant to follow is that the details in a story must support its headline—particularly if that headline makes an audacious claim. Two guys froze to death while looking for Bigfoot? Wow. Bring on the details.

    But that was the thing about the story of the Christmas Sasquatch hunters. After the stun-gun heds and ledes, there were no details about the supposed Sasquatch hunt. Not scant details. Not vague details. No details whatsoever. As if by mandate, every outlet that picked up the story made sure to include Sasquatch in its headline and opening grab. Then they dropped the Bigfoot angle altogether.

    Recent findings suggest that how long had the men been out looking for Sasquatch? Did they have a track record as Sasquatch hunters? Were they carrying special equipment, such as video cameras, long-range microphones, or telephoto lenses? If they were out searching for Sasquatch in rugged terrain and winter conditions, why were they so ill prepared?

    On these and other questions related to the Sasquatch hunt teased in the headlines, every story was the same—strangely mute.

    Excerpted from Sasquatch Country: Death, Myth, and Truth in the Upcoming American Wilderness by Chuck Thompson via Counterpoint Press.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Carla Magaly Alcedo Mendoza (Alcedo), 45, of Lima, Peru, was sentenced today to eight years in prison and three years of supervised release for overseeing a years-long transnational fraud conspiracy that used government impersonation tactics to defraud thousands of consumers across the United States.
    • “The Justice Department is protecting U.S.
    • “These criminals preyed on hardworking Americans, using fear and intimidation to steal millions of dollars.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Carla Magaly Alcedo Mendoza (Alcedo), 45, of Lima, Peru, was sentenced today to eight years in prison and three years of supervised release for overseeing a years-long transnational fraud conspiracy that used government impersonation tactics to defraud thousands of consumers across the United States.

    “The Justice Department is protecting U.S. consumers from fraudsters no matter where those fraudsters operate,” stated Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “We will continue to work with our partners at home and abroad to ensure that those who impersonate U.S. government and court officials to steal from Americans are brought to justice.”.

    “These criminals preyed on hardworking Americans, using fear and intimidation to steal millions of dollars. They deliberately targeted Spanish-speaking communities, impersonating government officials and threatening innocent people with arrest and legal consequences,” said Acting U.S. Attorney Yara Lorenzo Klukas for the Southern District of Florida. “Today's sentence sends a clear message: no matter where you operate, if you target Americans, we will pursue you and bring you to justice.”.

    “Today’s sentencing of the fourteenth defendant charged in this investigation was made possible by the outstanding collaboration between Miami Division Postal Inspectors, the Justice Department, and our international partners,” remarked Inspector in Charge Bladismir Rojo of the U.S. Postal Inspection Service (USPIS) Miami Division. “Transnational criminal organizations who victimize our citizens are not beyond our reach.”.

    Recent findings suggest that according to court documents, Alcedo was the operator of a Peruvian call center that defrauded and extorted U.S. residents by falsely threatening them with arrest, court proceedings, and immigration consequences. Alcedo admitted that she owned and operated a call center in Lima, Peru, that placed unsolicited calls to Spanish-speaking consumers in the United States and falsely claimed that they had won or qualified for free products, including computer tablets and English language courses. On later calls, Alcedo and her co-conspirators falsely claimed that victims were contractually obligated to pay large sums of money to receive the products. Alcedo and her co-conspirators impersonated government officials and lawyers to intimidate victims and force them to pay. Alcedo and her co-conspirators also threatened victims with court proceedings, arrest, and other legal consequences if they did not pay. The scheme spanned several years and thousands of victims made payments to Alcedo. Collectively, the scheme was responsible for defrauding more than 30,000 Spanish-speaking residents of the United States out of $15 million.

    Alcedo was extradited from Peru in April 2025 and pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit mail and wire fraud in August 2026.

    It has been revealed that including today’s sentencing in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida, 14 defendants have now been convicted and sentenced in connection with this scheme. The 14 defendants include 10 Peruvian call center owner-operators and four distribution center owner-operators who processed payments, distributed products, and facilitated the fraud in the United States, and a telephone service provider who facilitated the fraud schemes across the call centers in Peru. Alcedo and many of the defendants shared strategies on how to defraud consumer victims across the United States.

    In a recent development, alcedo is the 10th defendant charged in this scheme to be extradited from Peru and sentenced in federal court. In 2021 and 2022, Henrry Milla, Carlos Espinoza, Jerson Renteria, Fernan Huerta, Omar Cuzcano, Evelyng Milla, and Josmell Espinoza received sentences ranging from 88 months to 110 months in prison. In 2024, Jose Alejandro Zuñiga Cano was sentenced to 98 months in prison.

    Criminal Division Senior Trial Attorney and Transnational Criminal Litigation Coordinator Phil Toomajian prosecuted the case and Assistant U.S. Attorney Annika Miranda for the Southern District of Florida is handling asset forfeiture. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs, U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Florida, State Department’s Diplomatic Security Service, U.S. Marshals Service, Peruvian National Prosecutor General’s Office, and Peruvian National Police provided critical assistance with the case and extradition.

    This case is part of efforts being undertaken by the Department of Justice Criminal Division’s Cyber-Enabled Scam Initiative (CSI). The CSI is a dedicated team of prosecutors built to find scammers who prey on Americans, disrupt their networks, and hold them accountable. CSI brings together expert prosecutors from across the Criminal Division to accelerate the prosecution of cyber-enabled financial crimes, including complex frauds, government imposter schemes, romance and inheritance scams, financially motivated sextortion, lottery and sweepstakes scams, and other predatory schemes. With nationwide jurisdiction and global reach, CSI leverages every available tool to dismantle criminal operations, pursue bad actors, recover criminal proceeds, and obtain justice for victims. The Criminal Division partners with U.S. Attorneys’ Offices across the country and is a founding member of the Scam Center Strike Force.

    #43979. Tech Report: 5 gloriously unhinged speculative mysteries and thrillers

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1163 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: 5 gloriously unhinged speculative mysteries and thrillers

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1163 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, when a reviewer raved about my upcoming thriller, The Sleeper, with the words, “I love whatever is wrong with her,” I was delighted.
    • In a recent development, but this is not a modern phenomenon, there is a rich literary tradition of wild and crazy thrillers.
    • Robert Louis Stevenson, Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, when a reviewer raved about my upcoming thriller, The Sleeper, with the words, “I love whatever is wrong with her,” I was delighted. It’s my eighth book. With each one I’ve taken a bigger, bolder, and yes, a more unhinged swing. And I’m not alone. There is a rabid pack of unhinged thriller writers out there, and we’re only getting more bananas.

    In a recent development, but this is not a modern phenomenon, there is a rich literary tradition of wild and crazy thrillers. In fact, I’ve found it incredibly hard to whittle this list down to just five. This list bounces between the new, the nearly new and the really rather old.

    Robert Louis Stevenson, Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde.

    Industry observers note that one of those novels so powerful that it becomes a conceptual byword (by-phrase?) used even by people who have never read it. Published in 1886 and so brisk it’s actually a novella, this unflinching gothic masterpiece still holds its own in 2026.

    There is almost as much mythology about the writing of the book as is contained in its pages. Stevenson claimed that it sprang from a wild nightmare that contained three scenes and the central idea, “of a voluntary change becoming involuntary.” His step-son claimed it was written in a three-day fit of pique. His wife claimed that Stephenson burned the first version after she suggested he was writing an allegory, which riled him up before he realized he agreed, and then started again.

    Sources indicate that stephenson’s health at the time was dire, he was on medication to stop his lungs hemorrhaging, which could have stimulated the originating nightmare. According to some rumors he was also taking cocaine, which could also explain the mad work rate and agitation….

    If you haven’t read it recently (or perhaps ever), you may raise an eyebrow at its inclusion in a list of thrillers but it more than earns its place.

    We have unreliable characters, memory blackouts, dual personalities and a race to stop a killer. And it’s actually, I would argue, a speculative thriller given that the whole problem starts with Dr Jekyll experimenting to create a serum that can overcome the dark parts of his personality. Instead, the serum splits him into two—the good Dr Jekyll, and the evil Mr Hyde.

    Sarah Pinborough, Behind Her Eyes.

    Industry observers note that I know this came out nearly ten years ago but I’m still agape at its twists. Sarah Pinborough tore up the rule book with this one, and proved that you could still find fresh ways to shock a savvy audience of thriller readers.

    If you’ve not read it, I don’t want to give anything away but what starts as a tense psychological thriller about a single mum having an affair with her boss while forming a close friendship with the boss’s wife, soon takes a hard swerve into lucid dreaming, astral projection and a past timeline exploring trauma and mental illness. And if that sounds heavy and gloomy, I’m doing it a massive disservice because it is an absolute rollercoaster.

    The ending was so WILD that it was a key part of the marketing, with the hashtag #WTFthatending spreading through Book Twitter (this was 2017, after all…).

    Lisa Jewell, None Of This Is True.

    As a long-term fan, I loved watching the queen of women’s fiction become the doyenne of domestic suspense before winding her way down an ever-darker garden path. But Lisa Jewell’s 2023 novel, None Of This Is True, was a real escalation.

    Recent findings suggest that A fever dream of lies, paranoia and platonic limerence. Alix is a successful true crime podcaster who meets her “birthday twin,” Josie, an unassuming local woman born on the same day but whose life is very different.

    Recent findings suggest that they both have secrets, of course, which I’m loathe to give away but the novel is unflinching around dark topics like grooming, alcoholism and family dysfunction. For all its sucker punches (and the twists are *brain exploding emoji*) this is a nuanced and heartfelt exploration of the stories we tell ourselves in order to survive.

    In a recent development, if you were an unemployed gambling addict unable to pay your debts and whose loved ones were being threatened by the Yakuza, you’d take the first well-paid job that comes your way too, right? In this case, as a private chef to a reclusive billionaire in remote Japan.

    Soon, protagonist Ed is somewhat learning on the job in the best kitchen money can buy at the heart of an enormous mansion, with an endless supply of whatever ingredients the esoteric tastes of his boss desires….

    It’s been likened to Butter by Asako Yuzuki and there are overlaps in themes of greed, obsession and—of course—murder, but while Butter is a slow burn, Greedy is a runaway train. Messy, freaky and eye wateringly gory. I mean all those things as compliments!

    Fiona Cummins, Serial Killer Survivors Club.

    While 1980s teenager Robyn reels from the discovery that her father was a serial killer, her life is made infinitely worse by community ostracism and judgement.

    Sources indicate that an experimental therapy group for the familial survivors of murderers changes her life, finally giving her the acceptance and friendship she has always craved. But when one of her newly introduced friends disappears in a town where three other young women are already missing, Robyn and her found-family risk everything to find them. After all, with their intimate knowledge of killers, the Serial Killer Survivors Club are the best hope these missing women have….

    According to recent reports, I pat myself on the back for my ability to predict twists but this one spun me for a total loop. I was lucky enough to grab an advanced readers copy of this, which will be published next year in the UK and US. I highly recommend pre-ordering.

    My own unhinged thriller, The Sleeper, follows librarian Maya who falls asleep on a sleeper train and wakes up in a version of the world where history has changed overnight, her own life has been erased and nobody remembers her.

    Recent findings suggest that and the version of Britain she’s now living in? Just saying the wrong things can put you in the crosshairs of the state. Which is a massive problem for Maya, who in her bewilderment, has asked way too many questions already….

    According to recent reports, holly Seddon is the author of several thrillers, including the international bestseller Try Not to Breathe, The Hit List, and 59 Minutes. After growing up in the English countryside obsessed with music and books, Holly worked in London as a journalist and editor. After several years in Amsterdam, she now lives in Kent with her family and writes full time. Find out more at HollySeddon.com.

    #43978. Sacha Naspini on the human stories behind Italy’s tomb-raider subculture.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2229 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Sacha Naspini on the human stories behind Italy’s tomb-raider subculture.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2229 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, tuscany, 1972.
    • Recent findings suggest that when Bardo suddenly disappears, his son, Veleno, takes over the family business and old relationships between the gang and the milieu in which it operates begin to fray.
    • Sources indicate that sacha Naspini’s compact and suspenseful new novel, The Witch’s Mouth (2026, Europa, translated by Clarissa Botsford), drops you in the midst of the action, and creates a world peopled with crooks and cooks, a prostitute, heir-apparent, fishmonger, marquis.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, tuscany, 1972. Bardo Sacchetti has the people of the Val di Cornia wrapped around his little finger. Thanks to him and his band of tomb raiders, locals in the impoverished region can now buy fridges for their homes or give their kids an education. He asks for nothing in return except for gratitude.

    Recent findings suggest that when Bardo suddenly disappears, his son, Veleno, takes over the family business and old relationships between the gang and the milieu in which it operates begin to fray. Former alliances fall apart and Bardo’s empire looks like it might be destroyed by violence. Veleno has some massive decisions to make.

    Sources indicate that sacha Naspini’s compact and suspenseful new novel, The Witch’s Mouth (2026, Europa, translated by Clarissa Botsford), drops you in the midst of the action, and creates a world peopled with crooks and cooks, a prostitute, heir-apparent, fishmonger, marquis. The story unfolds from their perspectives.

    I sent written questions to Naspini, and Edoardo Andreoni translated his written responses from Italian into English. The interview has been edited for length.

    Sources indicate that radha Vatsal: Let’s start with some background. Tuscany, where the novel takes place, seems to be littered with antiquities. Is this more the case in Tuscany than in other parts of Italy? Can you describe some of the types of antiquities that have been found there in recent years?

    Sacha Naspini: Actually, that’s true of pretty much all of Italy. It’s a country where history has accumulated over millennia, layer upon layer. Here, even a routine excavation can turn into an archaeological discovery.

    It has been revealed that tuscany is no exception. In fact, it’s one of the regions where this historical layering is particularly evident, largely thanks to the Etruscan civilization, which preceded Roman rule. Discoveries are still being made today. Take the recent finds at San Casciano dei Bagni, near Siena: extraordinary bronzes, along with coins, crowns, jewelry, votive arms and heads….

    As for The Witch’s Mouth, the novel is set in a specific part of Tuscany, the Val di Cornia. It’s an area I know well, one that plays an vital role in the fictional universe of some of my novels. This was once home to Populonia, one of the most important Etruscan cities and the only one built directly on the coast. In the Gulf of Baratti, you can visit Etruscan necropolises, monumental tombs, burial chambers carved into the rock, and the remains of Etruscan and Roman settlements.

    RV: The events in the novel occur in the early 1970s. Was there a particular reason for choosing this time period?

    In a recent development, SN: Yes, there is. Choosing this period was an exciting challenge, and one that felt necessary. The Witch’s Mouth was born out of long conversations with tomb raiders and smugglers who were active during that time. Suddenly I came across some truly extraordinary, almost unbelievable stories. That’s when I began thinking about using this material as the basis for a novel.

    There were also three aspects that I found particularly fascinating. First of all, the “fever” I always noticed in the people who told me about their adventures. That’s the expression they would use: “digging fever.” It went beyond money or swashbuckling adventure—a special light would sparkle in their eyes. As these small-town Indiana Jones recalled those times, that almost addictive excitement was rekindled— the excitement of the moment when, after devising a strategy, they would finally manage to break into a burial site, the first people to set foot there in millennia. And then reach out and touch the objects… Part of my job was to try to capture their passion.

    It has been revealed that the second aspect was even more intriguing and had to do specifically with the Val di Cornia. The trafficking of archaeological artifacts was already underway in other parts of Italy—for instance in the Tuscia region—but in this small corner of Tuscany, people were late to the game.

    I heard crazy stories of farmers whose cellars were filled with bronzes that had turned up when they were plowing the land, and who would give them to their grandchildren to play with, like toy soldiers. After storms at sea, amphorae would wash up on the shore at Baratti. Kids would place them on top of low walls and throw rocks at them. Women would show up at Mass on Sunday wearing earrings and necklaces found in the fields….

    So I wondered, what would happen if an entire community, largely made up of people who struggle to make ends meet, suddenly realized that their homes were full of objects they considered worthless but that could fetch millions on the black market?

    As I was researching the historical archives of the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera, I came across a news story from 1971 about a twelve-inch bronze artifact seized by the Carabinieri. It was about to be sold to an American collector for half a billion lire (roughly $5 million in today’s money). People in that region had piles of similar bronzes, tossed aside in a corner.

    Industry observers note that finally, a purely personal aspect. I spent part of my childhood and adolescence in that region. Other kids and I would form our own little gangs and sneak out of the house in the middle of the night armed, with ropes, shovels, and spades, and head off into the woods. We imagined we were living in The Goonies, but instead of searching for One-Eyed Willy’s treasure, we were searching for Etruscan artifacts. Thinking back on it, what mattered wasn’t so much finding something as the adventure itself. Entering the woods at night was a substantial challenge. And then the thrill of digging, without really knowing where to look… In a way, I think I experienced some of that same fever the “professional” tomb raiders talked about.

    According to recent reports, RV: The Witch’s Mouth is an ensemble novel with a lot of different characters, but it revolves around Bardo. He’s almost a godfather-type figure in the way he involves so many different kinds of people in his activities and spreads the wealth he earns. Tell us about your inspiration for creating him.

    SN: Everything that happens in the novel is inspired by the interviews I mentioned earlier. But the characters are entirely the product of my imagination, as are the main plot and the various subplots.

    When it comes to Bardo, I did a little “plundering” myself. Based on the stories I heard, I imagined this guy who, even as a kid, recognized the value of these artifacts, which everyone else treated like useless old junk taking up space.

    But Bardo is also a man of action, and a pretty clever one. He knows how hard life is for the families of Populonia. He starts getting them to hand over their “pieces,” as they call them in the trade, and then sells them to the more experienced tomb raiders in the Tuscia region, returning with the money. Real money, not a few pennies.

    Recent findings suggest that before long, everyone starts looking at Bardo like a sort of saint. Everyone is knocking on his door with an artifact in their hand. And Bardo is extremely good at weaving a network built on trust and gratitude. That means protection—Bardo is untouchable. This is something else that fascinated me: at least in the beginning, there wasn’t a gun in sight. But then the operation grows exponentially. Billions of lire start pouring in. And where there’s that much money, guns usually follow.

    RV: Of the novel’s many great characters, I was fascinated by Elisa, Bardo’s wife; Silvana, the prostitute; and the Marquis. As you write, do you have favorites? Do some of the characters come more easily to you than others?

    In a recent development, SN: Obviously I love them all, not only because of the role they each play in the story—a character is always an opportunity to explore different points of view, different lives and legacies… What I mean is, how does a particular character, with their own history, react to certain events? That’s part of the magic of writing. Especially when we explore uncomfortable aspects of human nature and relationships.

    Recent findings suggest that that said, among the characters you mentioned, Silvana and the Marchese have a special place in my heart. Silvana truly is the queen (I should say, the Principessa) of the novel. The Marchese, for his part, embodies a desperation that is part of the landscape and is compounded by his broken dreams, a desperation that still moves me. Although in the end… but I’d better stop here.

    RV: In many ways, this is the story of a gang of tomb robbers but it’s also the story of an ecosystem of stolen goods and people.

    According to recent reports, SN: I had some interesting experiences in this respect during the promotion of the book in Italy. Together with my Italian publishers, we had the wonderful idea of organizing some events in archaeological museums. Some of the events were fantastic. In other cases, though, for instance in Vetulonia, the director of the magnificent local museum declined to participate. He didn’t want to celebrate, right in a place designed to house Etruscan artifacts, a story about thieves who had deprived everyone of the opportunity to admire works of art and experience the sense of connection we can feel with the people who lived in distant times.

    But I’m not an educator; I’m a novelist. I try to make sense of the world through stories. Even if these stories are unsettling—in fact, all the better. What I’m saying is, “Hey, look, this happened too.” I’m saying, “Hey, look at how these people lived. How they reacted, what they dreamt about, what circumstances led them to make certain choices.” And I know very well that it’s wrong to prevent the public from viewing a work of art, locking it away instead in some billionaire’s safe.

    According to recent reports, I’ll go further. For me, the real damage inflicted by tomb raiders is not the sale of a particular artifact to a private collector. The real theft—and maybe it’s the novelist in me talking—has to do with removing a clue (the artifact itself) from the place where it was found, thereby interrupting a story. Otherwise, archaeologists would be able to tell us how people loved, what clothes they wore or what food they ate, what gods they worshipped, what stories they passed down in that very place. This is what they rob us of, to make a few million dollars. I hope that somehow, between the lines of my novel, this message comes across. But according to some museum directors, I’ve missed the mark.

    RV: Are there other novels or writers you draw inspiration from in your work?

    Recent findings suggest that SN: The list would be endless, stretching from my formative years to the present, now that I’ve just turned fifty. It would comprise all the different kinds of writing I’ve sought out, explored, and measured myself against. And yet I feel like I’m just starting out.

    Recent findings suggest that to mention some writers that have a place in my heart, in no particular order: Italo Calvino, Stephen King, Albert Camus, Joyce Carol Oates, John Steinbeck, Chuck Palahniuk, Beppe Fenoglio, Ágota Kristóf, Mikhail Bulgakov. If you asked me again a minute from now, the list would be completely different. I’m thinking of John Fante, or the fantasy novels I adored as a teenager. And what about Dumas and his Count of Monte Cristo?

    According to recent reports, seriously, I never know how to answer this question. But I think that each of these writers has given me a great gift: they “gave me permission” to be brave. To let my imagination spill onto the page, for what it’s worth. And all the voices that come with it.

    RV: What are you reading and/or working on at the moment?

    Industry observers note that SN: On my nightstand are books by David Szalay and Ernest Jünger—the latter a special gift I received, a book that I’ve already read but want to reread. Recently, I returned to John Fante’s Wait Until Spring, Bandini after many years—what a knockout. I don’t think it will ever get old. I also really loved Tiffany McDaniel’s The Summer That Melted Everything.

    On my computer is a novel forthcoming in Italy, Il ronzio (“The Buzzing”), which is in the final stages of editing. Of course, I’m also working on another novel. And I’m having fun writing the treatment for a TV series, which is due soon. And listen to this: after twenty years of writing books, for the first time ever, there’s a police inspector in one of my stories. I never would have imagined it.

    Recent findings suggest that radha Vatsal is the Film/TV Columnist for CrimeReads. She is the author of No. 10 Doyers Street and the Kitty Weeks mysteries, and her essays have appeared in the The Fresh York Times, The Atlantic, the Los Angeles Review of Books, and elsewhere. She holds a Ph.D. in Film History from Duke University. You can find her on Instagram or email: rvatsal@lithub.com.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 11, 2026, 12:14 pm CST.

    According to Law.com, the next phase will center on paying creditors—chiefly landlords—and collecting outstanding receivables. (Photo from Shutterstock).

    Partners at Weil, Gotshal & Manges have formally voted to dissolve the nearly century-old law firm.

    Law.com reported Tuesday that 97% of the firm’s partners approved the move, which came about two weeks after the management committee recommended it Oct. 28. A three-person dissolution committee will oversee the firm’s dissolution, while Weil Gotshal executive chair Barry Wolf will act as a special consultant through the end of the year and longer if the wind-down runs into 2027. The firm will also utilize restructuring officers from management consulting agency AlixPartners and Davis Polk & Wardwell.

    According to Law.com, the next phase will center on paying creditors—chiefly landlords—and collecting outstanding receivables.

    Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, Law.com added that Weil Gotshal restructuring chair Matt Barr and several bankruptcy lawyers are in advanced talks to join Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom, which would remove one of Weil Gotshal’s last high-performing groups. Neither Barr nor Skadden responded to Law.com’s requests for comment.

    Barr’s potential move would be the latest in a partner exodus that has helped bring down the once-venerated Wall Street firm. According to Law.com, the firm saw nearly 50 partner exits in 2026, with sources estimating at least $500 million in lost business.

    Rivals race to rescue Weil Gotshal lawyers as firm heads toward closure.

    LiveKit is building the infrastructure layer for the agentic era of computing.     We're hiring a Solutions Architect (Pre-Sales) to be the technical partner to the engineers and enterprises building on LiveKit.

You'll collaborate closely with our Sales, Engineering, Product teams to win technical decisions and to make sure what you hear in the field informs how we build.

    love to build and solve the most challenging customer problems with LiveKit.

    have a curious mind with a continuous desire to learn and improve.

    Advise customers on cloud architecture and deployment across self-hosted and LiveKit Cloud (AWS, GCP, Azure).

    Scope and run proofs-of-concept against clear, shared success criteria, guiding customers all the way to production.

    Reason with customers about connectivity, infrastructure, and end-to-end latency to design for scale and reliability.

    Strong programming ability in at least one of our core SDK languages — Python, TypeScript/Node, or Go.

    A clear communicator who can demo, present, and write for technical audiences.

    Working knowledge of real-time media protocols and their latency/quality trade-offs (WebRTC, RTP/SRTP, WebSockets).

    Familiarity with the AI voice stack: STT/TTS providers, LLM integration, speech-to-speech models, turn detection, and telephony/SIP.

    Experience speaking at meetups or conferences, or a track record of technical writing or open-source contributions.

    An opportunity to build something truly impactful to the world.

    Contribute to open source alongside world-class engineers.

    Competitive salary and equity package.

    Sources indicate that liveKit is an equal opportunity employer and does not discriminate on the basis of any characteristic protected by applicable law. If you require a reasonable accommodation during the application or interview process, please contact recruiting@livekit.io.
